entries.title: DoorDash Cuts Grocery Reorder Latency from 16 to 2 Seconds with AI Agents
entries.summary: DoorDash reduced grocery reorder latency from 16 to 2 seconds by precomputing recurring purchase needs using batch LLM inference and deterministic validation. Live catalog resolution keeps product selections current, while an editable shopping interface avoids unnecessary model calls. The company reports that shopping list views doubled and the flow’s order rate increased by approximately 34% By L
entries.content:
DoorDash cut latency in its AI-powered grocery reorder flow from about 16 seconds to 2 seconds by precomputing recurring purchase needs instead of rebuilding them with each request. The change doubled shopping list views and increased the flow’s order rate by approximately 34%. The implementation builds on DoorDash’s shared agent platform and grounded shopping interface, which provide reusable agent infrastructure and let consumers modify shopping lists directly.

The implementation combines batch large language model (LLM) inference, deterministic validation, and live product catalog resolution within Ask DoorDash, the company’s conversational shopping assistant. Previous InfoQ coverage described how Ask DoorDash uses specialized agents and tools to support conversational discovery and shopping. For grocery reordering, DoorDash processes 90 days of purchase history alongside consumer profile signals. Batch LLM inference identifies likely recurring purchases, while deterministic validation checks the generated results before storing reusable shopping list data.

DoorDash’s grocery reorder architecture (Source: DoorDash Blog Post)

The serving path retrieves this prepared data and resolves each item against the current catalog. It first tries to match the original store item, then a catalog product identifier, and finally a search term. This allows the system to accommodate changing listings and unavailable products without repeating historical reasoning for every request.

The shared platform provides orchestration, memory, model access, tracing, evaluation infrastructure, and rollout controls. Domain teams retain ownership of agent instructions, skills, tools, and evaluation criteria. DoorDash reports that adding its Reservations agent took one week, approximately ten times faster than building its initial domain agents.

Ask DoorDash shared agent platform architecture (Source: DoorDash Blog Post)

Twisha Jain, a DoorDash engineer, described the design rationale in a LinkedIn post:

Better agentic systems aren’t always about more reasoning; they’re about deciding what belongs in the agent loop and what can happen ahead of time.

Moving recurring purchase analysis offline reduces the work required during a live request while retaining current catalog information for product selection. The system still invokes the Grocery agent for requests requiring additional reasoning, such as finding cheaper alternatives based on current prices, promotions, package sizes, inventory, and consumer preferences. Simpler operations, including changing quantities or removing products, update the shopping list directly without another LLM round trip.

A DoorDash engineering post about its shopping interface states:

A consumer’s direct edit is authoritative: the next agent turn starts from the edited list, not from what was said earlier.

The design treats the shopping list as a structured artifact that both the consumer and agent can update, rather than relying solely on conversational history. Other grocery platforms also use AI to personalize shopping. Instacart’s AI shopping assistant supports meal planning, list creation, and product discovery using consumer preferences and local grocery offerings. DoorDash’s implementation focuses specifically on reducing reorder latency by separating historical purchase analysis from live product resolution.

entries.title: Netflix Treats GPU Reliability as a Distributed Systems Problem
entries.summary: Netflix has detailed how it is building a reliability platform for large-scale GPU training and inference, using layered health checks, automated remediation, and fault-tolerant training to keep jobs running despite hardware failures. By Craig Risi
entries.content:
Netflix has detailed how it is building a reliability platform for large-scale GPU training and inference, using layered health checks, automated remediation, and fault-tolerant training to keep jobs running despite hardware failures.

The problem is particularly acute for large AI training jobs. A model may run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs, with all workers operating in lockstep. A single failed GPU, degraded network adapter, or slow machine can therefore stop or significantly slow the entire workload. Netflix has built its GPU compute platform on Kubernetes and designed it to detect these failures, remove unhealthy capacity automatically, and allow long-running jobs to recover from machine loss.

The approach has produced measurable results: Netflix reports more than 99.95% GPU-node availability and an increase in job success from approximately 98% to more than 99.5%.

A conventional cloud health check can establish that a virtual machine is running and reachable, but that does not mean its GPUs are capable of running a distributed training workload.

Netflix found that a GPU can respond normally to a status query while failing once memory is allocated or sustained computation begins. Similarly, a network adapter may be present but have fewer links than expected, allowing collective operations to continue at severely reduced bandwidth.

Device-level checks use NVIDIA DCGM to monitor GPU errors, memory, interconnect, and thermal conditions, while networking checks inspect the state and number of high-speed Elastic Fabric Adapter interfaces. A Kubernetes node agent converts these results into node conditions that controllers can act upon.

The checks are deliberately designed to fail closed. If a diagnostic tool hangs, its timeout marks the machine unhealthy rather than allowing a broken check to report success. Netflix also maintains fallback paths using kernel logs when the normal GPU diagnostic mechanism itself fails.

Detecting a fault is only half the problem. Netflix has built controllers that progressively respond to failures rather than immediately replacing an entire machine.

A transient problem can initially block new work while allowing existing workloads to continue. If the condition persists, the machine is drained, and its workloads are moved. Depending on the failure, remediation can range from killing a problematic job or resetting a GPU to rebooting the machine or replacing it entirely.

This approach integrates with Karpenter's node auto-repair capabilities, with Netflix adding policies that determine how long to tolerate different failures and how much of the cluster can be disrupted at once.

Netflix also accepts that hardware failures cannot be eliminated. Instead, its training platform makes them cheaper to recover from.

Large jobs use checkpointing and elastic workers, allowing training to resume from the last healthy checkpoint when a machine is lost. The platform can then automatically retry failures, while application failures are classified separately to avoid repeatedly restarting jobs with genuine software bugs.

Netflix also treats the training job itself as a distributed system. Rather than looking only for failed machines, it can identify a single slow rank that is holding the rest of the job back. This matters because a GPU does not have to fail to reduce the throughput of a synchronous workload.

Netflix is also using NVIDIA's Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) capabilities to allow smaller inference workloads to share GPUs while maintaining memory-level isolation between tenants.

This improves utilisation compared with dedicating an entire GPU to every workload. Netflix is also working towards Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), which should allow more expressive resource requests and topology-aware placement, including ensuring that GPUs, network adapters and CPUs are positioned appropriately within the machine.

Meta also uses extensive hardware diagnostics, automated remediation, checkpointing, and rapid recovery. Its recent work focuses heavily on detecting hardware faults, including difficult silent data corruption (SDCs), across extremely large AI clusters. Meta reports that hardware failures accounted for more than 66% of training interruptions in its Llama 3 experience.

Netflix's architecture places particularly strong emphasis on closing the operational loop: validate hardware before scheduling, monitor it during execution, identify the failure domain, remediate automatically, and measure the resulting goodput. Meta, meanwhile, has invested heavily in hardware-level fault detection and cluster maintenance as well as recovery.

Both approaches reflect the same underlying reality: at thousands of GPUs, reliability can no longer be treated as simply keeping individual machines available.

entries.title: Presentation: The Ladder Is Missing Rungs: Engineering Progression When AI Ate the Middle
entries.summary: Alasdair Allan discusses empirical research from METR and Anthropic on AI coding adoption. He explains the "supervision paradox," where reliance on AI tools disrupts junior skill development, risks institutional context loss, and threatens the long-term engineering pipeline needed to oversee autonomous systems effectively. By Alasdair Allan
entries.content:
Transcript

Alasdair Allan: Not 5 years ago, but 12 months ago now, almost to the day in fact, someone else stood up at an entirely different conference in New York, and during their talk they said this. They said that within 12 months AI will write essentially all of the code. I'd expect some of you in here today still write code, or at least some of you run teams that still write code by hand, like savages. The person who said this was Dario Amodei, the co-inventor of RLHF, the training technique behind virtually every modern AI, and the co-founder of Anthropic. He said that within 3 to 6 months, AI will be writing 90% of all the code, and within 12 months, virtually entirely all of it. At the six-month mark Amodei claimed vindication saying that 90% figure was absolutely true, at least within Anthropic. Twelve months on, almost to the day, and that's not exactly what happened, is it?

A detailed analysis by Redwood Research concluded that the 90% number he quoted was misleading. If you count only code committed to repositories, it was closer to 50%, which, at least to me, is still a pretty shocking number. The figure inflates to 90% only if you include throwaway scripts, one-off explorations, and all AI-generated text that was ever even transiently useful. Meanwhile, at the same time, Google reports that there just over 25% of internal code was AI-generated. Microsoft reports about 30%. GitHub Copilot shows roughly a 30% enterprise suggestion acceptance rate. These figures haven't really changed over the last six months, and that's nowhere near essentially all.

AI is writing a lot of code. The landscape of what being a developer is has massively changed. I think we can all acknowledge that. Amodei isn't making it up, Anthropic's own internal data shows engineers using Claude at 59% of their daily work, and self-reporting 50% productivity gains. Roughly 4% of all GitHub commits are now authored by Claude Code. The tools are real. The productivity is real in certain contexts. The problem is that writing code was never the point of our profession. That might surprise some of you. The conversation most people are having right now is about AI writing code. The conversation we should be having and are starting to have is around what software engineering looks like when software engineers don't have to write code. This talk isn't about either of those conversations. Instead, it's the question that both sides arguing about code are ignoring.

The structural question behind all of that. If AI handles the work that used to train engineers, where does the next generation of engineers come from? Amodei's own caveat to his claim last year proves the point. He said that programmers still need to specify the overall design, how code collaborates, whether the design is secure. He separated the writing from the engineering. Up until about three to six months ago, the writing was how people learned to do the engineering. Back in July last year, a Reuters headline got posted to pretty much every engineering Slack in the entire world. AI slows down some experienced software developers, study finds. As an ex-journalist, I don't consider that the most snappy of headlines, but it certainly grabbed everyone's attention. The METR study behind it, a proper randomized controlled trial, not a vendor survey, found that experienced developers using AI tooling took 19% longer to complete tasks. Before it started, they predicted the AI would make them 24% faster. After finishing, they still believed they'd been 20% faster. The gap between perception and reality was 43 percentage points. This headline alone challenges the narrative around AI. It's what happens next after this that really matters.

In February this year, METR tried to run a follow-up study. They couldn't. Not because the methodology failed, but because developers now refuse to work without AI. They couldn't find anyone to take part in the study. An increasing percentage, an increasing share of developers told METR that they wouldn't participate in any study that required them to complete half their tasks without AI assistants. The study became unmeasurable not because the effect had disappeared, but because the dependency had become too deep to control for. You can't do a controlled trial if there's no control. In less than a year, we went from AI makes experienced developers slower, but they don't notice, to developers wouldn't even attempt to work without AI. The tool went from optional to load-bearing before anyone figured out what it was actually doing to the people using it. Something worth noting about recent improvements in AI coding is where they are coming from.

To be clear, the last four to five months has seen what I consider a breakthrough in usability for coding tools. A significant part of that is the tooling and architectures around the model. Agentic loops, structured feedback from linters and test runners, the ability to iterate rather than generate in a single shot. The models got somewhat better thanks to targeted training by the AI companies. The scaffolding around them got a lot better. Most of the gains we've seen in the last four or five months, and they have been very large, have come from tighter feedback loops, architecture, not intelligence.

Act II - The Data

For the last year, I've been an interim CTO at a scale-up, one of our portfolio companies. I've been doing a lot of hiring. Anyone that's done a lot of hiring and done it for a year must know my pain. Anyone that hasn't done hiring, don't do hiring. Anyone hiring right now has seen it. Candidates with apparently impressive portfolios that fall apart under questioning. Or perhaps worse, are very obviously relying on AI augmentation during their actual interview. I built this now means I prompted this. Not always. Some people are genuinely learning. The signal is noisy. It's getting harder to tell who actually understands what they've produced. That's what made me really start worrying about what's going on here, about the ladder about career progression. I went looking for data. Not vendor surveys, not blog posts, and definitely not LinkedIn hot takes. Actual research with statistically significant results.

Harder to find than you might think, or possibly quite as hard to find as you might think. Fewer people doing it than you might think. METR again. They benchmark something they're calling the 50% task-completion time horizon. The length of a human calibrated task that AI agents can complete with 50% reliability. Their headline finding, the length of the tasks AI can handle entirely autonomously, without any intervention, single-shot, has been doubling roughly every seven months since 2019. Accelerating to roughly every four months since 2024. This y-axis here is a log scale. It's the success rate. It's this success rate where the career ladder breaks. Here we have Claude Sonnet model's successful probability plotted against human task duration. The S-curve drops off sharply after about an hour. The curve is at nearly 100% for tasks a junior developer would do in their first year. Nearly 0% for tasks that require judgment built on years of doing those junior tasks.

For tasks that would take a human under four minutes, so small bug fixes, boilerplate, simple implementations, AI can now do these with a near 100% success rate. There's no point giving these to a human. The AI can do it faster and more reliably, autonomously. However, for tasks that will take a human around an hour, AI has roughly 50% success rate. For tasks over four hours, below 10% success rate. That said, these benchmark scores dramatically overstate real world capability. METR's own mergeability study found that roughly 50% of all AI-generated pull requests that passed the automated tests would not actually be merged by most repository maintainers. On 18 real tasks for mature open-source projects, Claude 3.7 Sonnet passed test cases, but 38% of the time produced zero mergeable PRs out of the 15 reviewed. Every single PR had at least three categories of quality issue: missing documentation, inadequate test coverage, linting violations, or code quality problems. The average time the maintainer took to fix the AI-generated PR into a mergeable state was about 42 minutes, about a third of the total time the human would have done to do the task themselves. AI can implement core functionality, but consistently fails with craft, the exact skills the middle rungs are supposed to build.

Before we move on, I'll remind you of that METR study, experienced developers using AI tools took 19% longer to complete tasks. Before starting, they predicted AI would make them 24% faster. After finishing, they still believed they were 20% faster. Contrast this to a randomized control trial done by Anthropic, where 52 mostly junior software engineers learned a new Python library, Trio, which bills itself as a friendly Python library for async concurrency and I/O. The time it took them to do this with or without AI was not statistically different. A p-value of 0.391. These were not statistically different. The AI group was about two minutes faster, but that's well within noise. The group using AI did not get any meaningful speed boost to learning how this library worked. Anthropic's paper says this explicitly. The productivity gain from AI assistants on this task failed to reach statistical significance.

Despite the slight overlap in those error bars there on the right, the score they got on the mastery quiz afterwards to test their understanding of what they had learned during this process was statistically different. A p-value of 0.01, well below the 0.05 threshold. We see a significant decrease in library-specific skills, conceptual understanding, code reading, debugging amongst the group that was AI-assisted. The group using AI assistants scored 17% lower on the mastery quiz, 50% versus 67%. The largest gap was on debugging questions, the very skill required to verify the output from the AI in the first place. The AI group learned significantly less while not even finishing the task significantly faster. They didn't trade speed for learning. They traded learning for nothing. There was no tradeoff. There was just loss. There were three major failure patterns among those low-scoring participants. Full AI delegation. They didn't even try, they wholly relied on the AI from the start.

Progressive AI reliance. They tried for a little bit, and then they gave up, and then they relied on the AI the whole rest of the time. Interestingly, iteratively AI debugging. They used the AI to debug the AI's output rather than trying to understand what the AI had done. All the developers that fell into these three cohorts and exhibited these behaviors scored well below 40%, compared to 67% on the unassisted group. Anthropic points out this as a paradox explicitly. Productivity benefits may come at this cost of the skills necessary to validate AI written code if junior engineers' skill development has been stunted by AI use. They call it the supervision paradox. Effectively, using AI requires supervision, and supervision requires the very coding skills that atrophy from AI overuse.

Act III - The Human Cost

Data doesn't tell us everything, though. I saw a LinkedIn post by senior engineers with 25 years' experience in industry. For me, it actually really captured what the data doesn't. For anyone leading a team of engineers right now who are resisting AI tooling, consider what's really happening in their world. Their entire professional identity is built on top of a skill that is rapidly losing market value. The standard reassurance of, "You'll still be needed to design and architect everything, don't worry," doesn't really land, when 90% of your lived experience is the thing you supposedly no longer need. A few words around architecture are going to bounce off that. However, the pattern recognition these veteran coders carry, how systems should be structured, where complexity hides, and what breaks its scale, can no longer be acquired the traditional way. Junior engineers won't spend years reading legacy codebases or debugging production incidents at 3:00 in the morning.

We've all been there. They'll just point the AI agent at it and ask them to summarize. The deep intuition for how software actually behaves in the real world is becoming more difficult to obtain. Possibly now extinct outside a group of us who live for what will probably be fondly looked back on as the craft era. Empirical data supports this emotional narrative. Faros AI's Productivity Paradox reports, analyzing telemetry from about 10,000 developers across 1,200 teams, found that teams with high AI adoption completes 21% more tasks and merge 98% more pull requests. PR review time increases by 91%. Bugs per developer rise 9%. The average PR size inflates 154%. The bottlenecks don't disappear, it migrates upstream to code review, exactly where all of that senior judgment lives. Anecdotally, we've seen a number of high-profile open-source projects flat out ban PRs generated by AI. I don't blame them, but I also don't think it can continue forever. That surge in low-quality AI slop submissions has a significant problem for open source right now.

A report from DX of about 20,000 developers this time, dated from Q3 last year, so before the recent surge in quality from AI coding tools, shows the rate of adoption skews towards less tenured engineers, so the junior folks. Senior engineers, despite having the lowest adoption rates, who do use AI daily, save the most time. You're probably immediately going, what? Asking yourself the difference between this study by DX and the METR study I talked about earlier. DX surveyed 20,000 developers and found senior engineers report saving the most time. METR put 16 experienced developers under controlled observation and found they made them 19% slower, while they believed it made them 20% faster. Both of these things can be true simultaneously. The fact they can, it is in itself a real problem. If we can't even measure whether the tools are helping, how do we know whether the people using them are learning?

The METR study was of experienced developers working in codebases which they were deeply familiar with. These developers' skill sets were already highly optimized for those codebases. The data for the DX study covers work by a much wider sample of developers across their entire work week. Greenfield, unfamiliar codebases, boilerplate, documentation, the lot. AI does save time on some of this work. A lot of this is short, well-defined tasks that METR's own time horizon research shows AI handles well. While their headline-grabbing RCT report dealt with the isolated case where the AI helps least, experts on familiar ground with complex codebases. If we take a step away from that corner case, we see a pattern. AI helps the already skilled, while creating output without understanding for novices. The people who'd benefit most from deliberate practice are the most likely to skip it. That probably should surprise none of us.

Anthropic's own engineers narrate this in real time. One senior engineer said they used AI primarily in cases where I know what the answer should be, or at least vaguely know what it should look like. Noting they developed the ability to do that by doing software engineering the old-fashioned hard way. If they'd be earlier in their career, developing those abilities would have required deliberate effort to avoid blindly accepting the model's output. Another senior engineer at Anthropic described AI output as really smart in a dangerous way. The kind of thing a really talented junior engineer might propose, recognizable as problematic only by someone with deep experience. Anthropic's engineers report asking 80% to 90% of questions to Claude instead of their colleagues. One senior engineer said it's sad that junior people don't come to them with questions as often anymore. Although they definitely get their questions answered more effectively and more politely.

Possibly the really surprising thing for those that have worked in this space for a long while is that the senior engineers liked working with people and missed them when they went away. The incidental learning that came from human interaction, understanding how systems work by struggling through debugging sessions with a mentor gets bypassed when AI gets you the answer without that journey.

Act IV - The Case Study

I've shown you a lot of graphs, but I think a recent problem presents us with a rather elegant case study on what's going wrong, the Amazon incidents. Who's heard of what's going on with Amazon right now? Yes, it's interesting. In mid-December 2025, AWS engineers allowed Amazon's Kiro AI coding tool to make changes to AWS Cost Explorer. The AI agent, given operator-level permissions equivalent to a human engineer, decided the best approach was to delete and recreate the entire environment rather than make targeted changes. AWS spent 13 hours recovering Cost Explorer in one of two China regions. Amazon called it user error, specifically, misconfigured access controls. Four sources later told the Financial Times that Kiro autonomously made that decision. A human engineer, one would hope, would know that delete and recreate the entire operational production environment is not a sane response to a configuration change. That knowledge comes from having seen things go wrong, from having lived through production incidents, from having absorbed the implicit rule that you don't blow away state in a production customer-facing environment.

AI had the permissions. It lacked the battle scars. Then, interestingly, came a series of outages on the Amazon retail site. Over 22,000 people reported issues during a roughly six-hour disruption on the 5th of March. Both the FT and the CNBC reported the internal briefing documents identified GenAI-assisted changes as the contributing factor. With a trend of incidents characterized by a high blast radius, a novel GenAI usage for which best practices and safeguards are not yet fully established. Five days later, on the 10th of March, SVP, Dave Treadwell, made normally optional, This Week in Stores Tech, TWiST meeting mandatory. His email apparently began, "Folks, as you likely know, the availability of the site and related infrastructure has not been good recently." Multiple news outlets then reported that Amazon had introduced new approval requirements. Junior and mid-level engineers were now required to seek senior sign-off on AI-assisted production changes.

Like that METR study, the story went around pretty much every engineering Slack channel in the world, some of you have come across it. However, interestingly, in the last few days, Amazon has really pushed back against this narrative. In a public statement, they said the FT reporting contained inaccuracies. Their version was that only one of the recent retail incidents involved AI tooling in any way. That incident was not caused by AI-written code. Instead, it was an engineer following inaccurate advice that an AI tool inferred from an outdated internal wiki. The other outages were separate, unrelated operational issues with no AI involvement whatsoever. No new approval requirements for engineers using AI tools had been introduced. Amazon characterized the AI-involved incident as human error, not AI failure. Amazon says that most of these outages have nothing to do with AI. Maybe they're right. I'm quite willing to believe them.

Look carefully at what Amazon did confirm. An AI tool read an outdated internal wiki. It inferred advice from stale documentation. An engineer followed that advice. The site went down. That's not a story about AI writing bad code, it's a story about context. The AI couldn't distinguish current wiki page from an obsolete one. It couldn't assess whether the advice it was synthesizing still applied to the systems as it exists today. It treated everything in its context window with equal weight because that's what these tools do. The engineer who followed the advice either didn't have the experience to question it or trusted the tool's confidence, and we all know how confident those models can be, far more than their own uncertainty.

As I said at the start of this talk, the problem was never writing code, it was always about what surrounds the code. The design decisions. The system context. The accumulated understanding of why things are the way they are. An outdated wiki page is a failure of institutional memory. The engineer who follows its advice without questioning it is a failure of judgment. Both of these failures map directly to missing rungs. A reliance on AI rather than your own judgment. An arXiv paper from last month tracked how teams manage AI context. One project evolved into 26,000 lines of codified context, more instructions than actual code. Meanwhile, an analysis by GitClear of 211 million lines of code showed AI tools adoption increasing code volume by 10%, but collapsing quality metrics, refactoring dropped by 60%. Copy and paste rose by 48%. Code churn jumped by 44%. The models writing code with less understanding of what already existed.

This is the distinction between prompt engineering, how you ask, and what we now call context engineering. What the model sees as it starts working. The teams that get this right, treat context like infrastructure, files that read like onboarding documents, memory hierarchies with progressive disclosures, architectural decisions recorded with reasoning behind them. The 26,000 lines of context architecture is not overhead, it's the institutional knowledge that used to live in people's heads, made explicit so that AI can use it too. New engineers can learn from it. Because most engineering is not greenfield, it's brownfield or what some people have started calling blackfield. Legacy systems under high load, on a deprecation path everyone agrees on but literally no one has time to execute. Been there. Features still being bolted on because the business can't wait. In blackfield systems the spec was never written or was written and made totally irrelevant by decades of undocumented decisions.

Business rules are encoded in conditions that outlived everyone who understood them. AI agents can read the code, tests and documentation but what they can't do is read production. They can't look at years of request patterns and understand which code paths are load bearing in ways the code themselves does not reveal. They can't distinguish a dead edge case from one that runs for 0.1% of your users, every single one of whom will immediately complain as soon as it disappears.

Amazon's outdated wiki is just the most visible form of this problem. Every codebase is full of implicit knowledge that hasn't been written down or perhaps worse yet was written down once and never updated. The AI can read what's there, it can't know what's missing or stale. Only someone who's lived with the system can do that. The honest sequence for non-greenfield systems isn't write spec, generate code, run tests. It's, observe production, extract behavioral contracts, encode the system tests, use that for the spec, and then bring in the agent. The tools for this already exist, characterization tests, contract testing, traffic shadowing, canary analysis. These aren't new ideas by any means. They're what software engineers worked out before AI entered the picture. AI conversation needs to inherit them rather than pretend the problem is being solved by better prompting. Whether you believe the FT's version or Amazon's version, the structural point is the same.

AWS Kiro incident, delete and recreate, is what happens when AI agents have permissions without judgment. Judgment that comes from years of production experience. Confirmed retail incident, the outdated wiki, is what happens when context isn't curated. Context curation is exactly the kind of institutional knowledge that the missing rungs were supposed to build. The dispute itself reveals how organizations resist framing these as structural problems. Amazon called it user error and routine operational review. In engineering, following confidently wrong AI advice from stale documentation is not a one-off mistake. It's a pattern that will reoccur everywhere AI tools are deployed into systems with institutional memory gaps, which pretty much is every large corporate system ever. The question isn't whether Amazon's outages were caused by AI. The question is what happens when AI tools are deployed into environments where the context they need, the production knowledge, the institutional memory, the understanding of why things are the way they are, lives in the human heads that were built by decades of doing the work AI now handles. Where does that context come from when the people who would have built it never did the work in the first place?

Act V - Mind the Gap

I'm not going to try and give you a part answer. As an industry, we are facing a fundamental structural problem. The ladder is missing rungs. Of course, the interesting thing is we've been here before. In the 1980s, the home computer revolution created a generation of engineers who learned by tinkering, my generation. We were brought up in the BBC Micro, the Commodore 64, the ZX Spectrum, the Trash-80, machines that booted to a basic prompt or CPM if you were really lucky. Kids wrote games, tools, experiments, mostly rubbish, but we learned. By the early 2000s, computers had become sealed appliances. Desktops booted into Windows, not to a prompt. Games came on disks, then over the internet. They definitely did not come with source code anymore. The Xbox replaced the BBC Micro in most homes. The ability for kids to write at home in their bedroom a game or an application that was just as good as a professional software house could.

That's something that happened a lot in the 1980s. A lot of the games sold in cassette tapes to kids like me were written by other kids in their bedrooms. That was now gone. Then by the mid-2000s, computer science departments started noticing that incoming students had never written code before coming up to university. They'd used computers their whole lives, but had never programmed one. They didn't understand how they worked. This started a mass panic in both academia and industry. There were a whole bunch of initiatives designed to deal with the problem. One of the more prominent ones was Raspberry Pi. Raspberry Pi was an explicit response, a deliberate recreation of accessible tinkering. Not, we need a cheap computer. That was the solution. The problem was, how do we get kids access to a machine they can own completely, that it didn't matter if it broke? One that boots to a prompt that had GPIO pins to allow them to touch the physical world.

It worked. Millions of units, a generation reintroduced to tinkering. It wasn't the only thing that was pushed to solve this problem, but it was one of the more prominent things. Physical computing, making an LED flash on and off again, was the new write-your-own video game. Not least because for a brief time in the mid-2010s, kids, or at least young adults, university students, could build or at least prototype IoT devices in their bedroom or dorm room that was just as good as us professionals could, just about. It took years of thinking about the problem before building the solution, and it only worked because the diagnosis was right.

The current AI disruption is the exact same dynamic, but at the professional level, rather than with the kids before they even get to university. The scut work that built engineering teams, bugs, boilerplate, glue code, documentation, is now handled before juniors ever see it. Anthropic's internal data quantifies the new shape of engineering work. Engineers report using Claude in 59% of their daily work, up from 28% a year earlier, achieving a self-reported 50% productivity increase, although do bear in mind the studies I talked about. More than half say they can only fully delegate about 20% of their workload. One engineer estimated that their role had shifted to 70% from being code to being a code reviewer reviser, not a code writer. Claude Code autonomous actions doubled from 9.8 to 21.2 between February and August last year, while human turns per transcript fell from 6.2 to 4.1. The work that remains is increasingly supervisorial, architectural, and judgment heavy.

Now there's evidence that the pipeline isn't just failing to build judgment, it's failing to hire the people who would have built it. At the start of this month, Anthropic published its own labor market analysis, Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence. The paper introduces a new measure called observed exposure that combines theoretical LLM capability with actual Claude usage data, weighing automated and work-related uses more heavily. The report makes interesting reading. Computer programmers are the most exposed occupation at 74.5%, meaning three-quarters of our programmers' daily tasks are now seeing significant automated usage in real world professional settings. At the other end, 30% of workers have zero coverage, cooks, mechanics, lifeguards, and bartenders. My parents told me not to become a lifeguard. The physical world remains untouched, at least for now. Although I'm not sure given the opportunity to comment back in the late '90s in the heat of the first dot-com boom before the bust, I would have predicted Uber. Given the effect the internet and the iPhone, which really did change everything, folks, would have on taxi drivers.

AI is far from reaching the theoretical capabilities. The gap between what LLMs could theoretically do and what they actually are being used for remains large. Computer and math occupations have 94% theoretical exposure, but only 33% observed coverage. The red area, actual usage, is much smaller than the blue area, theoretical capability, across every occupational category. This is a modest gap from the start of the talk, measured precisely. Occupations with higher exposure are projected by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the U.S., the BLS, to grow less through 2034. For every 10 percentage points increase in AI task coverage, the government's growth projection drops by 0.6 percentage points. The labor market analysis is already pricing in job displacement. However, there is no systemic increase in unemployment for highly exposed workers, yet. The unemployment rate for AI-exposed occupations has not diverged from baseline since ChatGPT's release. This is important.

The sky has not fallen. The doom predictors are wrong so far. The hiring of young workers has slowed in exposed occupations. New job stats for 22 to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations visibly diverge downwards from unexposed occupations starting in 2024. The average estimate is a 14% drop in job finding rate, not advertisements, finding, in exposed occupations compared to pre-ChatGPT levels. There is no decrease in work for workers over 25. This is just for junior developers just joining the industry. The result is barely statistically significant, but it echoes independent findings from another report based on ADP payroll data. That survey found a 6% to 16% fall in employment in exposed occupations from workers 22 to 25, again, primarily being driven by slowed hiring rather than increased separations. People weren't being sacked. They just weren't being hired in the first place. This is the missing rungs thesis measured in the labor market in real time.

The rungs aren't just losing their educational function, the jobs themselves are contracting. Companies aren't firing experienced workers, they're not hiring the next generation. The pipeline is being cut off at the intake, not the output. Once again, it's Anthropic publishing this. The company that builds Claude is documenting the evidence that Claude's adoption correlates with reduced hiring in young workers in the most exposed professions. Three studies from the same company. AI stunts skill formation, AI transforms work into supervision, and now AI slows hiring at the entry level. Whatever you think of the emotives, their intellectual honesty is remarkable.

Every source, including Anthropic's own internal research, agrees on this. The organization is racing to adopt AI coding tools that are simultaneously degrading the pipeline that produces people capable of supervising those tools. The people who can build good context for AI are people that have the context in their heads through years of craft. The pipeline that produced these people is breaking. If you come here hoping for me to hear an answer to this, I'm really sorry to disappoint you because I don't have one. There are no easy answers because right now I don't have a Raspberry Pi piece shaped to fit the AI shaped hole. There are some things we can do now before we have the answers. Structured learning paths, deliberate rotation through fundamental work, even if the AI could do it faster, like medical residencies. You do the scut work because it teaches you, not because it's efficient.

Require understanding before letting the AI help. It's expensive and most companies won't do it. The ones who do will be the ones who have senior developers left in 10 years because the rest of us will have retired by then. There's a reason why medical doctors are trained how they're trained. Measure understanding, not velocity. Can you explain what code does? Can you debug without AI? What happens if this fails? Pair programming is evaluation. Watch how they think, not what they produce. Treat context as infrastructure. The teams that get AI right are treating codified context as teaching documents, not config files. The best ones read like onboarding docs for a senior engineer who already knows how to code but doesn't know your codebase.

We have entered an era of documentation first programming. I find it somewhat ironic that the part that most developers hate has become the whole job. As an ex-docs person, I'm really happy. Beyond that, we need honest expectations. Tell the juniors that AI is a tool, not a teacher. Using it to skip understanding is borrowing against your future. The people who are valuable in 10 years are the ones who understand the systems, not ones who can prompt. Going back to the original METR study and making wild, waving extrapolations at the current doubling rate, AI agents will handle tasks equivalent to a full work day by 2027, and a work month by 2029. Take that with more than a pinch of salt, mind you, because personally I don't believe we'll ever get there. Even Moore's Law broke eventually. At that point, the middle rungs aren't just missing, the ladder is being rebuilt against a different wall.

If you have 10 bakers producing 1,000 loaves a month and new ovens let 5 of them go on and do the same job, you either cut staff or bake more bread. Anthropic's data offers one possible escape, 27% of Claude-assisted work comes from tasks that would not have been done without AI. New experiments, nice to have tooling, exploratory work, not baking faster, but baking things that weren't previously worth baking. Writing code is a huge bottleneck, was a huge bottleneck. Software started out custom developed in companies for their own use. It became a mass-produced commodity when demand grew past available supply. The entire SaaS market sits on the shoulders of shortage, a shortage of developers, of time to build the perfect custom solution for every problem. Instead, we're stuck with spreadsheets and web applications designed for most cases.

I'll give you a personal example. Over the last few months I've been building a programming language, Vera, designed specifically for AI-generated code, a language designed for machines to write. It's exactly the kind of project I wouldn't even be worth attempting without AI tooling. A single person building a compiler, a type system, a test suite, a conformance framework, that used to take a village. Historically, new technology means more productivity, not less jobs. Right now, the labor market data says the city is choosing fewer bakers. Amazon laid off 14,000 corporate workers in October, 16,000 more in January. Anthropic's own observed exposure data shows the BLS projecting weaker growth for most AI-exposed occupations. The question is not whether to adopt AI. That's a closed question. We're going to adopt AI. If you think you or your company won't, then you won't have a job or a company in 12 months from now.

The real question is, how do we build engineers, ones that can supervise what they have never learned to do in the first place? If we don't solve that problem, nobody will have a company in 10 years' time, because the ladder isn't just missing rungs, it's missing the mechanism that created the people who built the ladder in the first place.

Questions and Answers

Participant 1: One thing that I noticed is that your presentation relied heavily on AI-generated content. According to your own self-reported estimate, how much time did you save and how much did it make you faster? I also want to ask in terms of effectiveness, how much do you think it helped understand your content?

Alasdair Allan: Actually, for me, always the most time-consuming thing has been creating amusing slides to fill the slide deck with. Midjourney is a savior for me. It cuts my time creating a presentation by at least 20%. That's how much faster it's going to be. There was a lot of numbers in this slide. Yes, I found all of these using AI. That's not true. A lot of them surfaced in my feed, and I read them, and I fed them into the AI to try and get a synthesis of them. You've got to believe, I checked every single number that I said today. You've got to believe that I went to every single reference and made sure it actually existed. That's because 25, 30 some years of bitter experience in the industry. Yes, AI may have been creating the talk faster. It made finding sources and synthesizing those sources and see how those came together easier. Didn't write the talk. I still did that. I think it proves the thesis of the entire talk.

entries.title: Netflix Titus Adds Single-Tenant VM Isolation for Containers
entries.summary: Netflix has added single-tenant Titus, a mode that runs one task alone on its own right-sized EC2 instance. The Compute/Platform team still owns and patches the host, so application teams keep the same API and deployment path By Claudio Masolo
entries.content:
Netflix has added single-tenant Titus, a mode that runs one task alone on its own right-sized EC2 instance. The Compute/Platform team still owns and patches the host, so application teams keep the same API and deployment path. First adopters include stateful, high-throughput streaming workloads. Here, a neighbor's interference can lead to minutes of checkpoint recovery.

Titus launches millions of containers a week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances and is multi-tenant by default. Netflix says that cgroups, seccomp, the iocost controller, and traffic shaping can’t split shared hardware. This includes resources like the last-level cache and memory bandwidth. Its HTB traffic shaper also takes a global lock. A container that floods the host with small packets can burn the kernel CPU and starve its neighbors. Predictive CPU pinning and eBPF-based detection helped, but Netflix concluded that shared-kernel tuning narrows the gap without closing it.

Netflix rejected the alternatives for specific reasons. MicroVMs such as Firecracker and Kata need bare-metal or nested virtualization, and nested virtualization was not ready on Netflix's instance types. They also meant running a hypervisor layer, added virtualization overhead, and lacked GPU support. gVisor added overhead on I/O-heavy paths, and a single vendor does most of its maintenance. Running containers on EC2 would hand host patching and fleet sizing back to application teams. Netflix argues that these workloads require performance isolation, not defense against hostile tenants.

The Titus federation layer does most of the work. An allowlist, maintained by the Compute/Platform team, controls eligibility and federation records, which instance families a task may use. The autoscaler launches the smallest instance that fits the task's CPU, memory, and GPU request. Pod anti-affinity, a non-preemptible priority class, and a node taint enforce one task per node. Netflix disables defragmentation, so nothing relocates the task. To measure isolation, Netflix runs a reference app alone, then beside a "havoc" container, and scores retained throughput and P99 latency. The post publishes no scores.

Launch latency is the main cost. A fresh instance needs tens of seconds to boot before the image pull begins. Warm pools help less than on the shared fleet, because right-sizing produces many instance shapes. Netflix keeps a small warm pool for the most latency-sensitive starts and limits the available sizes. It dropped metal instances for these pools. Disabling Kubernetes preemption removed a scheduling bottleneck that left new nodes idle. Lazy image pulling (stargz, SOCI) and CRIU checkpoint restore are longer-term fixes.

Efficiency can improve. Moving sensitive workloads off shared hosts removes the anti-affinity spreading and disruption budgets that left those hosts partly empty. Fixed overhead from sidecars and system services pulls the other way. Netflix says it can cost a small instance tens of percent of its resources, and the largest shapes only a couple of percent. Discrete EC2 sizes also leave bin-packing gaps on large shared hosts, which favored right-sizing in practice.

Early users include managed Apache Flink, streaming data connectors, and telemetry and logging pipelines. Then, there are some latency-sensitive GraphQL and edge services. The rollout continues. For the shared fleet, Netflix is working on eBPF-based Expected Departure Time shaping to replace HTB, plus cache and memory-bandwidth partitioning (Intel RDT, AMD PQoS), NVIDIA MIG, and the cgroup v2 IO controller. Its long-term goal is one Compute API that picks EC2 or Titus placement from declared intent.

Single-tenant Titus joins a broader set of approaches to the same problem. Instance-per-Pod Webhook, an open-source project from NTT’s Akihiro Suda, uses a Kubernetes admission webhook and the Cluster Autoscaler to create a tainted, dedicated instance for each pod. AWS Fargate makes the pod the unit of infrastructure, so customers do not create, patch, or scale worker nodes. GKE offers sole-tenant nodes, dedicated physical servers that run only a single project’s VMs, along with GKE Sandbox, which runs each pod in its own Kata Containers microVM. Azure’s Pod Sandboxing is also built on Kata and gives each pod its own lightweight VM, isolated from other pod VMs and the host kernel. Most of these target security isolation from untrusted code, while Netflix’s post focuses on performance isolation between trusted internal teams.

Teams running shared Kubernetes platforms can borrow the pattern: dedicated node pools with taints, anti-affinity, and repacking turned off. Netflix recommends it for large, long-running, disruption-sensitive workloads sized close to a node shape and not for small or bursty services. The allowlist keeps the mode from eroding multi-tenant density.

entries.title: Article: InfoQ AI, ML and Data Engineering Trends Report - 2026
entries.summary: This InfoQ Trends Report offers readers a comprehensive overview of emerging trends and technologies in the areas of AI, ML, and Data Engineering. This report summarizes the InfoQ editorial team’s and external guests' view on the current trends in AI and ML technologies and what to look out for in the next 12 months. By Srini Penchikala, Chip Huyen, Daniel Dominguez, Hien Luu, Arthur Casals
entries.content:
Key Takeaways

  • Language models have shifted from large-sized models to the small language models. We are also seeing the rise of reasoning models that can think through math and logic problems before responding.
  • AI Agents are moving from personal agents to the agents working with teams to companies using agents across entire organizations.
  • System One models like TypeSafe AI’s Jev will see more adoption because of their deterministic and faster inference, in addition to their lower costs compared to the LLMs.
  • AI Inference continues to be a useful and powerful trend and more and more companies will start doing this moving forward.
  • AI evaluations have been getting a lot of attention this year. Evaluations are a way to help us to make sure that the agents do the right thing for the right tasks.
  • Physical AI has seen significant developments in 2026. We are starting to connect the software intelligence to machines that can perceive and act in the physical world.

The InfoQ AI ML Annual Trends Reports offer InfoQ readers a comprehensive overview of emerging trends and technologies in the areas of AI, ML, and Data Engineering. This report summarizes the InfoQ editorial team’s podcast with external guests to discuss the trends in AI and ML technologies for the year 2026 and what to look out for in the next twelve months. In conjunction with the report and trends graph, our accompanying podcast features insightful discussions of all of these trends.

AI and ML Trends Adoption Graph

An important part of the annual trends report is the trends graph, which shows the trends, technologies and topics that have made it to the innovators category and which have been promoted to the early adopters and early majority categories. The categories are based on the book, Crossing the Chasm, by Geoffrey Moore. At InfoQ, we mostly focus on categories that have not yet crossed the chasm. Here is this year’s graph:

It has been almost four years since ChatGPT came out back in November 2022. It has also been two or three years since RAG Technologies started seeing enterprise adoption and autonomous LLM agents came out. The explosive growth of the last few years has continued in 2026 and AI technologies have seen significant innovations and developments since the InfoQ team discussed the trends report last year (see 2025 trends graph below).

For the details of 2025 AI ML technology trends, also check out last year’s trends report article.

This year’s trends article builds on what we discussed last year. It highlights the trends graph, which shows different phases of technology adoption and provides more details on individual technologies added or updated since last year’s trends report. We also discuss which technologies and trends have been promoted in the adoption graph. For this year’s updated adoption graph, the team has also added a few additional topics that we didn’t discuss in the podcast.

As you will notice, we have also done some major reorganizing of the topics where there is an overlap of the scope, and removed a few technologies that no longer need to be tracked on the adoption graph because of their mainstream adoption.

Here are some highlights of what has changed since last year’s report:

Innovators

The first category on our adoption graph, Innovators, has a few interesting new topics added this year. These topics are discussed in detail below.

Agent-to-Agent Protocols

As agentic AI systems become complex involving multiple different agents and domains, the communication between the individual agents as well as between multi-agent systems is crucial for these systems to be consistently safe, accurate, and reliable.

One of our panelists in the trends report podcast, Daniel Dominguez, spoke about agent communication protocols and the significance they have in the overall agentic AI solutions.

Daniel Dominguez: There is an architectural shift happening underneath all of this. For agents to become useful inside enterprises, they need to access tools, data, APIs, and talk to other agents. All the protocols like MCP or A2A are going to become more and more different. I think the question would be whether agent protocols become a new enterprise integration layer.

For example, today we connect applications to APIs. Tomorrow we may increase and have agent discovery capabilities that we see in task coordinating work on top of those APIs. I think all of these architectural layers are also changing the way that agents interact with each other.

Inference Engines (vLLM, SGLang, llm-d)

Another area that saw a significant development and transformation is the AI Inference. 2026 has been called the year of inference. The companies are shifting from training models to running AI inference in production. Inference is expected to account for around two-thirds of AI compute spending by the end of this year. Reasoning models, long context, and agents have turned it from a model-execution problem into a systems problem spanning compute, memory, networking, routing, and economics.

Hien Luu discussed this trend in detail in what he is seeing in terms of inference frameworks.

Hien Luu: The inference topic has exploded since the beginning of 2026. Obviously from one end, you have all these inference stacks from vLLM, SGLang, and so on that are helping the rest of us to spin up our own inference service in our own environment. At the same time, these open-weight models are becoming more and more capable. That space is initially not a whole lot of people how it works and how to operate it, but now there's a lot more information and resources out there about how to actually use these software, [and] how to optimize them. At the same time, some of the use cases we talk about are the financial companies where you have PIIs.

The ability to host these open-weight models internally for those kinds of specific use cases are very, very relevant. I believe that that's going to continue to grow, continue to be the case where a company will do more of this moving forward now that it's a lot more approachable, easier to do. There are some companies that because they want to save cost, they actually want to host internal open-weights models for coding, for example. For many reasons that inference is going to continue to be a very, very useful, very powerful topic and more and more companies will start doing this moving forward in my mind.

Harness Engineering

A relatively new area that has been seeing a lot of attention starting this year is Harness Engineering. Hien talked about the importance of this topic and how it supports the engineering capabilities like memory management and co-execution.

Hien Luu: I want to add [two things] to discussions of agents. One is harness engineering. I think that extensions of context engineering. But the thing that I see is quite interesting and relevant to a workshop that I'm going to be giving is that these agent SDKs start out with just helping us to write the loop. Now this SDK has been expanded to provide harness engineering capabilities, including memory management for context, including co-execution, including some of the out-of-the-box tools for doing into actual local file systems.

That’s another trend you can see that these agent SDK from LangChain or Anthropic or OpenAI; they all move in that direction of adding more capabilities as part of the harness engineering. As anyone building agents moving forward, that's something to look out [for] and leverage. There’s a whole other trend of managing these agents. These companies are providing a runtime environment for you to host your agent. Whether you want to do it or not, that's a separate question, but that's what they're seeing. "We are able to build, we are able to build it well, and then how do we operate and run it at scale?"

Spec-Driven Development and AI Software Factories

With AI technologies contributing to most of the coding in the software development process, we are seeing the developers starting to focus more on the requirements and specifications to take full advantage of automating the design and coding tasks in their applications.

This technology shift has given rise to trends like Spec-Driven Development and AI Software Factories. Some organizations are creating dedicated teams to create the software factory model where the development teams can use AI tools to automate the complete software development process. This model includes the specific SDLC steps like automatically compiling and analyzing the business domain and requirements of an existing software application, reviewing the new business requirements or systems enhancements, writing functional and non-functional (technical) specifications for those new requirements, generating the design and development tasks to implement the new requirements, and, finally, auto-generating the code and other artifacts of the updated software application.

Panelist Hien Luu shared his insights about Spec-Driven Development.

Hien Luu: This probably started maybe four or five years ago. The coding agent now is pretty powerful. But as you build a project, typically you want to have a plan in advance in terms of what you want, the capabilities and whatnot, and not jump to the coding agent immediately to build. It is borrowing what we know as a good practice to do, but now codified it in a form for the coding agent that you work with. If you build a brand new greenfield project, for example, you build a spec up, what is it about? What are the capabilities that you want?

Then you have a brainstorming session with your coding agent to provide a context that it needs before you actually go and build it. I think there's a lot of good practices there that people have built around this. I think most people recognize that's a good practice. I don't hear much more about it now because as people are actually practicing it and the AI factory is another that's probably in the last few months of really how to infuse AI into the various steps of your software development life cycle.

The typical use case is, "Hey, somebody raised a bug. How do you get AI to take that from beginning to end to actually take the PR, do an analysis, try to recreate the problem, come up with a fix, submit a PR, and then you go through the rest of the steps of review and testing and so on?" That is as we all have too many things to do, too many tasks. I think if we can help automate that, that will accelerate another dimension to accelerating the software development life cycle.

Physical AI / Embodied AI

Another area that continues to see more and more innovation is Physical AI. This is where we bring intelligence into the real world. An AI agent is a software system, how do we bring the same power into the hardware, whether they're robots or collaborative robots (cobots) or self-driving cars.

Daniel Dominguez talked about what's happening and what we should be paying attention to in the Physical AI world.

Daniel Dominguez: Basically it's saying, "How do we bring AI into the physical world?" Over the last few years we have spent the time putting intelligence into software. Now we're starting to connect that intelligence to machines that can perceive and act in a physical world. So what, you said, we are starting to see robotics, we're starting to see autonomous vehicles, drones, and industrial systems are now part of this transition. What I think makes physical AI fundamentally different from software agents is that mistakes have physical consequences on the physical AI.

One thing is that in software, an agent can make a mistake generating their own file, but a robot can move their own equator. It’s going to be a whole different level of mistakes. Reliability, simulations, safety, verification, [and] evaluations are going to become more and more important in the physical world. Based on that, all the foundation models for robots that are happening right now, another important shift is that robotics are starting to benefit from more of the same foundational model approach that transformed the language and vision.

We're going to start seeing things like [a] simulation for digital twins robots, all the things that are going to happen for open robotics, [and] all the things that are going to happen from AI agents to physical agents. All of this is just going to start moving faster and faster over the next year because right now the AI is here. Now we have to put it in our physical world.

Chip Huyen also discussed how robots and vision language models can work together.

Chip Huyen: It's the next frontier to get the models into the real world and we see a lot of progress. I think the only challenge is that there are several challenges. We keep saying that robotics are like cars, like LLM to say, "Okay, we know we have a lot of robots in the real world." We have Waymos everywhere. We have Zoox. We see a lot of robots in the real world.

One big difference between robotics, models, and LLMs, it's that the challenge of backtracking. For LLMs, when you're training on a virtual, on the computer, if it makes a mistake, you can run back. You can reset the state and continue. You can do a lot of explorations and pick the best state.

You can't really do [that] exactly [in] robotics. You can't get a robot, "Okay, there's a staircase that's there". The robot falls and it breaks. You can't just run it back and get the same robot as before. It makes exploration extremely, extremely hard. Another challenge is data. I have been looking into a lot of robotic setups. I think Janatics Robotics company – we have a bunch of companies like Generalist, Physical Intelligence, Sunday, Skild AI, which I'm very excited about.

Other trends in the Innovators category we have added or revised for this year include the following topics:

  • Agent Security and Governance
  • Voice Agents
  • Specialized Decision Models (e.g., TypeSafeAI's Jev Model)
  • AI Gateways
  • GraphRAG
  • LLMOps / GenAIOps
  • Brain-Computer Interfaces

Early Adopters

In the Early Adopters category, we would like to highlight two main topics: Innovations in language models and RAG.

AI Agents / Agent Orchestration

Similar to last year, Agentic AI has again been the dominant topic this year. 2025 and prior years were all about how to learn and how to build AI agents. Now the organizations are trying to figure out how to operate the agents, how to deploy them to production, and how to scale them in production.

Daniel Dominguez discussed the recent developments in AI Agents area, in this year's podcast:

Daniel Dominguez: I think the biggest change in 2026 is that AI is moving from being something that we interact [with] to something that we delegate [to]. Like Hien was saying, I think most AI applications over the last few years were based on a simple interaction. You will just ask a question and the mobile gives you an answer. Right now we're starting this year, we are starting to see a system that can plan, can use tools, can execute actions, can do their own work and continue working for a much longer period of time. I think this year is less about another jump in the model intelligence and more about turning that intelligence into actual systems.

What I find interesting is that agents are moving through several levels very quickly. We started with personal agents helping one person, then we started seeing agents working with teams, and now companies are thinking about agents operating across entire organizations. I think the important change is that we're moving from beyond just a chatbot model. Instead, we are simply generating an answer. An agent can have goals, can use tools, can interact with software, can make decisions, [and] can keep working until the task is complete.

I think that changes AI from [an] interface into something closer to an execution layer. We can see this mainly in software development. Software development is probably where this transition is more visible. We moved from autocomplete to copilots and now we have coding agents. We have tools like Claude, Codex, Cursor, Replit, and others that can navigate repositories, can modify multiple files, can run comments, can execute tasks, can inspect failures, and can iterate on their own. The interesting question is no longer, can AI write code? We already know that AI can write code.

In the AI Agents space, more complex systems using multiple agents (multi-agent systems) are becoming more common because of the additional benefits they can bring to the table, compared to systems based on individual agents.

Panelist Arthur Casals spoke about the current research happening with multi-agent systems, how these multi-agent systems work, and what are the real-world use cases to leverage them.

Arthur Casals: When you think about multi-agent systems as a topic, it's been there for a few decades already before LLM agents. People from the academic community are seeing whatever comes with LLM agents and after transformers and is related to the entire multi-agent systems trying to reinvent things that were there in the past. My research area is on classical multi-agent systems, before LLM, which doesn't mean that it can't incorporate or use LLM systems as part of it. But these days I've been working on belief revision. This is a big part of solving two problems actually in the AI landscape, one related to hallucination and the second one related to information accuracy and provenance after being processed by the agent. It's between computer science and philosophy, a lot of formal logic, but yeah, it's really interesting. One thing that we've been working with, I think since the beginning of this year, and the end of last year, is a formal logic-based profile definition that could be used. It's similar to the concepts around Jev that we were discussing before. So [they] have a structure input, a structural output and how we can make the AI not the agents refrain from using agents, but actually working from here to there.

AI Evaluations for Models and Agents

This year, we have also seen more developments in the quality assurance space with the AI evaluations, guardrails and harness frameworks. The year 2026 has been dubbed as the year of AI Evaluations. There are a lot of different techniques that are gaining attention in this area. Testing harness frameworks are probably the most talked about topic this year. As AI tools are increasingly leveraged to write code and other components of software solutions, the need for formal, rigorous, consistent and reliable validation frameworks has never been more critical. How do we then measure AI effectiveness? What kind of metrics can help in the evaluation and validation steps with an end-to-end process that has proper checks and balances?

We asked the panelists to explain what they are seeing in the agentic AI evaluation space. Here are their observations.

Hien Luu: This is a very important topic for companies that are bringing their AI agents to production, particularly the one that for their customers, not so much about internal ones. If you look at an example from DoorDash, they build an AI assistant for ordering food. You have other companies that are building customer support agents for external users. We all know that LLMs are not deterministics and building agents, they can take the wrong turn, they can make the wrong tool calls and stuff like that. Evaluations are a way to help us to make sure that the agents do the right thing for the right tasks at the highest level.

Without evaluation, how would you know that it's gone rogue or does something that's unexpected, not according to your company's policies and all that stuff like that. Companies not only have to do this, but they have to incorporate this as one of their core steps in building AI agents. A lot of companies end up building something called an evaluation harness, which helps drive the whole evaluation flow from getting the data, running the evaluation or tests, as we all know tests – right? – and then assessing the quality at the end.

Daniel Dominguez: I completely agree with the idea that this year is becoming the year of evaluations for models and agents. Once an agent can perform an action, evaluating only the model is not enough. You have to evaluate the whole system, you have to evaluate the model, the tool, the context, the agent loop, the environment. Here is where the metrics changed as well.

It’s not only whether the answer was correct, it's whether the agent completed the task, how much it cost, how long it took, how many interventions were necessary, and whether it did something unsafe along the way. I think all these evaluations were just starting to see how we are going to evaluate all this workflow regarding agents and regarding LLMs and regarding the interactions that they do in our job.

Outside of these highlighted technology trends, there are a few entries that we are moving from Innovators into the Early Adopters category. All these technologies listed below have gone through extensive development and adoption and are now being used by many applications in various organizations.

AI technologies have, for the right reasons, started being leveraged in the DevOps and SRE areas of the production support, troubleshooting, maintenance, and upgrade operations.

  • Agentic Coding / Autonomous Software Engineering
  • Agent Observability
  • Inference Optimization and Model Routing
  • Small Language Models (SLMs)
  • Reasoning Models
  • Explainable AI
  • Virtual Reality (eg VR/AR/MR/XR)
  • Cognitive Services
  • Edge AI Inference
  • Model Context Protocol (MCP)
  • Multi-modal AI
  • AI DevOps/AI-powered SRE

Early Majority

We are moving the following topics to the Early Majority category as these technologies have become more mainstream and are being widely adopted by software development teams in various organizations.

Context Engineering

In the age of AI agents, Context Engineering topic continues to be important and evolving to be used in AI powered solutions. Arthur Casals spoke about this with emphasis on one of the challenges in Context Engineering, the Context Pollution.

Arthur Casals: Context pollution is actually the biggest problem, the problem worth emphasizing now, because we've seen the past year or so movements toward bigger context windows in general, but they don't really solve the issue if the system cannot distinguish what's useful, what's current, what's alternative information from irrelevant, stale, adversarial material. I'm bringing something from my own research here, but in general, more context can make an agent slower, more expensive, less reliable.

The practical question would be, if you have your context window, regardless of the size of it, what enters the context? From which source, with which permission, for what step of the workflow so you don't have this huge pollution. That talks about retrieval quality, source distribution, professions rules, context model in general, context compression. I mean, there's a huge, huge heap of problems underneath the word context. That's how I see it.

Also, compared to last year’s report, we have more topics as listed below, that we think are ready to move to Early Majority status.

  • Generative AI/Large Language Models (LLMs)
  • Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
  • Knowledge Graphs
  • MLOps
  • Vector Databases
  • Data Contracts
  • Data Observability
  • Graph Data Analytics
  • Synthetic Data Generation
  • Open Table Formats (OTFs)

Late Majority

Finally, in the last category in our adoption graph, the Late Majority, we have a few topics that have moved from the Early Majority category. These technologies are now fully adopted by teams and part of their core architecture and design patterns and development processes.

  • Automated Machine Learning
  • Image Recognition (Computer Vision)
  • Digital Assistants
  • Data Mesh
  • Stream Processing and Analytics
  • Recommendation Engines
  • Lakehouses
  • Spark

Topics Removed from Adoption Graph

We also want to note that in this edition of the AI ML Trends Report, we have removed some mature technologies that have been in use for several years now. These technologies have become very much part of the mainstream technologies and adoption, and don’t need to be tracked on our adoption graph for our readers.

Some of these topics include mature technologies like NLP and Deep Learning, NoSQL Databases, In-Memory Data Grids, and Big Data (Hadoop).

Conclusion

AI is a significant technology shift. As we all know by now, after almost four years, it is not a fad or some temporary blip on the technology radar. It is here to stay. It is one of the major technology waves in the last twenty-plus years. We should take advantage of this technology transformation, not be afraid of it. Find ways to use AI tools to automate any workflows in your day-to-day life, whether it is in the office projects or in your personal life.

Some of the team’s predictions for the next year include:

  • We expect to see more innovations in US-based robotic companies.
  • We will also see a lot of cheaper and faster models; the TypeSafe style of model would be very interesting.
  • We're going to start seeing limitations on AI, in the areas of energy and AI infrastructure in terms of access for electricity, capacity, and cooling data center locations. For 2027, some of the biggest AI stories may actually happen outside the models themselves; it's going to be more about energy, the chips, the infrastructure, and the geopolitics.
  • Every AI agent will incorporate some form of the Jev model.
  • Increasingly, communications are going to be between agents, moving forward as we figure out how to build, operate and bring all these agents to production.
  • We'll see a lot of things using smaller specialized agents for mixed models, for well-defined tasks. The big difference will be in the surrounding system.
  • AI will be even a bigger part of our daily lives. We think the niche areas will be settled where AI will be really valuable and where human intelligence is still required.
