entries.content:
In this episode of the podcast, members of the InfoQ AI and ML editorial staff and friends of InfoQ discuss the current trends in the domain of AI, ML and Data Engineering.

One of the regular features of InfoQ are the trends reports, which each focus on a different aspect of software development. These reports provide the InfoQ readers and listeners with a high-level overview of the topics to pay attention to this year.

InfoQ AI, ML and Data Engineering editorial team met with an external guest to discuss the 2026 trends in AI and ML areas, and what to watch out for the next 12 months. In addition to the written report and trends graph, this podcast provides a recording of a discussion where expert panelists discuss how innovative AI technologies are disrupting the industry.

Key Takeaways

  • Language models have shifted from large size models to the small language models. We are also seeing the rise of reasoning models that can think through math and logic problems before responding.
  • AI agents are one of the biggest trends of 2026. Agents are moving from personal agents to the agents working with teams, to companies using agents across entire organizations.
  • System One models like TypeSafe AI’s Jev will see more adoption because of their faster inference and lower costs compared to the LLMs.
  • AI evaluations have been getting a lot of attention this year. Evaluations are a way to help us to make sure that the agents do the right thing for the right tasks.
  • Physical AI has seen significant developments in 2026. We are starting to connect the software intelligence to machines that can perceive and act in a physical world.
  • Our panelists’ AI predictions for next year include: More innovations in US based robotic companies, cheaper and faster models, limitations on AI in the areas of energy and AI infrastructure, every AI agent will incorporate some form of the Jev model into the AI agents, applications using smaller specialized agents for mixed models, AI will be even a bigger part of our daily lives and niche areas will be settled where AI will be really valuable and where human intelligence is still required.

Subscribe on:

Transcript

Podcast and Panelists Introductions [00:38]

Srini Penchikala: Hello, everyone. Welcome to the 2026 AI and ML Trends Report Podcast. Greetings from the InfoQ AI, ML and Data Engineering team. We also have a special guest today for this year's trend report discussion. This podcast is part of our annual report to share with our listeners what's happening in the areas of AI and ML technologies. I am Srini Penchikala. I serve as the lead editor for the AI, ML and Data Engineering community on InfoQ. I will be facilitating our conversation today.

We have an excellent panel with subject matter experts and practitioners from different specializations in the AI and ML space. I will go around our virtual room and ask the panelists to introduce themselves. We will start with our special guest first, Chip Huyen. Hi Chip, thank you for joining us and participating in this podcast. Could you introduce yourself and tell our listeners what you've been working on?

Chip Huyen: Hello, I'm Chip. I'm very excited to be here today. It's an honor. I know that everyone on the panels has amazing background. I've been following your work for a long time. Today, I was hoping to share what I know, but also hoping to learn from you all. I'm working on a lot of AI stuff, AI agentic, getting AI to work well for workflow. I'm also very interested in making AI just faster and cheaper. We saw recently the TypeSafeAI that came out. I think there's a huge demand for cheap and fast intelligence, and that's very exciting.

Srini Penchikala: Thank you, Chip. Yes, definitely if we have time, I would love to learn more about this Jev model from TypeSafe AI, if you have any experience on that. Daniel, how about you?

Daniel Dominguez: Hi, I'm Daniel Dominguez. I'm the deputy editor at InfoQ. I focus on artificial intelligence, machine learning and data engineering. I'm also a software engineer and really particularly interested in AI agents, agentic software development and how AI is moving from pure digital system into Robotics and Physical AI.

Srini Penchikala: Thanks, Daniel. Arthur?

Arthur Casals: Hi, everyone. I'm Arthur. I'm a researcher and technology strategist, basically. And these days I split my time between consulting, advising companies about how to make AI useful in real systems and applying research basically on multi-agent systems and belief revision.

Srini Penchikala: Thank you. And, Hien?

Hien Luu: Hi everyone. My name is Hien Luu. I mainly focus on ML infrastructures as well as, I guess nowadays, agentic engineering. Currently, I'm helping with a startup on consulting on AI inference and a long-term fan of QCon, also an editor of InfoQ, also a QCon program chair for QCon AI New York.

Srini Penchikala: Yes, thanks, Hien. I am definitely very excited to talk with you all about this topic because you have been part of InfoQ and the QCon family for so long. It's always great to chat on these topics. So I'm looking forward to speaking with you about what's happening in the AI and ML space, where we currently are, but more importantly where we are going at the fast pace as the AI technology innovations keep happening since we discussed this report last year.

Before we start with the actual podcast topics, I want to go over a couple of quick housekeeping items for our audience. There are two major components to these trend reports. One is obviously this podcast, which is an opportunity for you to listen to the panel of expert practitioners and see how the AI innovations are disrupting the industry. The second part of the trend report is a written article that Arthur also mentioned that we can cover a lot more topics in that article.

So that will be available on InfoQ website along with the podcast recording. That's where we actually assess the current technology adoption and we have an adoption graph that we update every year to highlight which technologies are further ahead in the adoption cycle than the other technologies. It's always a great reference for anybody who is following the technology innovations in the AI space. Definitely look for those two parts, the podcast as well as the article. And also I definitely recommend that you check out all InfoQ publications.

In this podcast, we will definitely discuss the important developments in AI technologies that took place since our last report back in August last year. But due to a limited time in this forum, we won't be able to cover all the topics or even get into in-depth discussions on some of the topics, but we will try to follow up on those important topics as separate podcasts or separate articles because they're important for us to learn about. But again, I encourage you to check out the InfoQ website and AI and ML and data engineering community, which includes news items, articles, podcasts like this and presentations.

It's also worth mentioning with all the AI stuff happening that this podcast is not AI-generated or even AI-assisted. It is being recorded with real people who have real-world experience. I just want to get that disclaimer out of the way. So contrary to all the predictions being made out there that AI is going to replace everything. So that being said, let's get started. It's been almost four years since ChatGPT came out back in November 2022. It's been two or three years since RAG Technologies started seeing enterprise adoption and autonomous LLM agents came out. So definitely a lot of things have been happening.

State of AI in 2026 [05:58]

Agentic AI has been the main dominant topic for a long time now. So we'll definitely look at that a little bit today. We are seeing more developments in the quality assurance space with the AI evaluations and harness frameworks and all the other good topics. We'll get into more of those details later, but the first topic is I would like to get a quick take, maybe 30 seconds take from each of the panelists, on how do you see the current state of AI in 2026? Chip, could you start us off?

Chip Huyen: So it's going absolutely crazy. So I'm checking on the money in and out of the AI company. So money in, as in private investment and then money out, acquisitions and IPO. So for many, many years, we see the charts very similar, one of the three numbers because the money in has to come out at some point. But in recent years it's grow like this. The money in grow exponentially and the money out is no money out at all.

It's very exciting. It has the amount of money and it's I think proportional to, I guess I use as a proxy for people excitement. A lot of companies, the number of company size is going down as the average median company size going down significantly. So that means that people can do a lot of things that anyone can build nowadays. Anyone can have a product. So the issue is not really about how to build things anymore. Anyone can build things, but what you build and then how do we as a receiving end filter through all of that is insane.

And I think going through these things like winner-catch-all catch situations because a few products somehow still face and everyone just talks about them and the rest is lost in the shuffle. And it's very, very tricky. It's just like everyone is forced to face the same ideas and at the same time we have a lot of new things coming out, but somehow everyone's talking about the same thing. We don't get it. Yes, it's very, very strange.

Srini Penchikala: How about you, Hien, what are you seeing as AI in 2026?

Hien Luu: Yes, obviously like Chip said, there's a lot of excitements, innovations, product announcements, but if you want to talk about at the beginning of 2026 or the end of 2025, you're talking about the year of agents. I think we are in a phase where the AI agent stack is being built in a way, the different layers. There's a lot of progress there, a lot of exciting, a lot of innovations for all of us, how to learn, how to build AI agents.

And now everybody's trying to figure out how to operate them, how to bring them to production. So that's a very exciting space from an enterprise perspective. I think the other one that I'm sure everybody is aware of is writing code. It's easy now. We're coding agents. So I think there's many exciting ideas going to be built and we all need to adjust in terms of how we build software going forward. So I think that's another area that's happening in 2026 and we'll definitely see more excitement in 2027.

Srini Penchikala: I think we'll get into those topics a little bit more Hien later anyway, so we'll have time. So how about you, Arthur? What do you see at a high level?

Arthur Casals: Yes, I think - following up on Hien, I mean, I think what we're seeing now is we're changing or shifting our perspective from the parts of the car to the car itself. I mean, you have impressive isolated capabilities and each model will be developed year after year. And now you're starting to realize as companies in production that we need them to work and to be dependable.

So I mean, you can have a pilot of a great agent that can work beautifully, can have created data and that's great, but very good prediction that you have your data is messy, you have different permissions, you have regulations, the system has to be affordable, it has to be recoverable.

So that feels like the defining test for AI that we're seeing emerging right now is not whether it can do something once, but whether a team can trust it in a real workflow to solve real problems. So that's when you see it actually being applied in companies that have been successful.

Srini Penchikala: Thanks, Arthur. How about you, Daniel, what are you seeing?

Daniel Dominguez: I think the biggest change in 2026 is that AI is moving from being something that we interact to something that we delegate. Like Hien was saying, I think most AI applications over the last few years were based on a simple interaction. You will just ask a question and the mobile gives you an answer. Right now we're starting this year, we are starting to see a system that can plan, can use tools, can execute actions, can do their own work and continue working for much longer period of time. So I think this year is less about another jump in the model intelligence and more about turning that intelligence into actual systems.

Large Language Models (LLMs) and Frontier Models in 2026 [10:36]

Srini Penchikala: Thanks, Daniel. Thank you for that. Yes, that's a good segue from there. With AI agents and all the other innovations happening, the foundation is still on those language models. So maybe that's where we can start our main discussion today because there's always a lot of new developments happening there. So in 2026, my observation is the language models have shifted from these massive size models, billions of parameters into the smaller size models, small language models where they can be faster in terms of performance, may not be as accurate, but accurate enough for most of the use cases.

And also we are seeing the rise of reasoning models that can think through math and logic problems before actually responding. So a lot of good stuff happening. So we can start with this as the main topic. Arthur, I know you've been looking at some language model topics and also frontier models. So what do you see is happening here, what our listeners should be aware of or should be learning about?

Arthur Casals: Yes, I think in general, when you focus on specific models, we have better reasoning, we have better coding, we have better multimodal abilities. They're emerging, it's evolving. But then we're going to go back to what I said first, that if I were to pick a headline for frontier models in 2026, I'd say that the model itself is becoming less of the whole story. So you do have the capability, you do have to worry about it, of course, but we're changing the question from which model is best to which model or combination of models gives us the right capability, latency, data boundary, cost for this workload, specifically this workload?

Which, to me at least, the trend seems to be a move from choosing one model to delivering matching models to workloads, which makes it a system design question, not a model choosing question. And I see that as a sign that a field is maturing because the model stops being the whole problem and becomes the one component of the architecture. So we do have to worry about all the specific capabilities of each model, but they have to work in unison, together.

Srini Penchikala: Any other thoughts from anyone else on the models?

Chip Huyen: So I think that model size is a little bit interesting because the definition has changed over time because the model size, number of parameters, it also depends on how many of them are actually active at the same time. It's a trillion parameters model with only a few percentage. And also another is the quantizations. I do think this very, very exciting work on quantization recently. I feel like about two, three years ago, people thought it was crazy to have a 4-bit model, but now they have consistently see people running 1 to 2-bit model, which is a significant reduction in size. And we think of it as a compute requirement, a computer efficiency of these models.

So I think it's interesting to see. Another trend I see from models is that of a release cycle because let's say that you have a very, very strong model. You release this out at the top of every benchmark. And then a few weeks later it released another model much cheaper, smaller, almost like equivalent, but maybe 1 or 2% drop in performance. So I think this is usually a trend of yes, we have a big model and then you distill that into a lot of other techniques, like using a better mixture of expert, making it more sparse, quantization aggressively one time into a smaller and a cheaper model.

Hien Luu: Yes. There was a lot of interest in doing fine-tuning toward the beginning of the year, and there's a lot of innovation in that space with LoRA and all that stuff like that. And all these kind of neocloud inference providers started to provide the ability to do fine-tuning for at least the open source models. I would love to hear from the panel if you have heard successful use cases in the enterprises, they actually do fine-tuning for their specific use cases. I think there's some happening, but I don't hear much about it.

Obviously it takes a lot of effort to do that with the right skill sets, maintenance, operations, doing inference, the whole shebang. It's doable, but whether that is make you reliable and in operations and all that stuff like that is still a lot of work. So maybe things will be easier in 2027 and people do it more, but that's still a question in my mind of how pervasive that is being actually done in enterprises.

Srini Penchikala: That's a good point, Hien. How do you make the model management life cycle similar to software development lifecycle? How do we make it repeatable and streamlined?

Hien Luu: Exactly. Yes. Unlike traditional ML, you start with data and then you train and evaluation and then you bring it online and here you do fine-tuning. So it's a lot of work, but I'm sure there are specific use cases, particularly perhaps these AI-native company that in the domain of legal, Harvey and such. I'm sure they do fine-tuning there. But beyond that, I wonder if enterprises, they actually do it. That's my question.

Arthur Casals: I've seen a couple of companies doing that, but they're very specialized in what they do and they're very, very careful about IP. So they won't disclose that for a few years at least I think. But usually I'm seeing this basically in healthcare and finance. It's concentrated there for some reason. You know the reason, but yes, it's happening, just need the budget, but it's already happening. It's great.

Hien Luu: Makes sense.

Chip Huyen: Yes. I was just about to ask, has any of your company fine-tuned any model? Arthur mentioned it's waiting for budget, it's supposed to be expensive?

Arthur Casals: I think it depends on what you're doing, how you're doing it. For example, when you come to open models, I've seen a small rush of open models and local models and people thinking that, "Okay, it's going to be cheaper". But think about open. When I have the word open, I have open weights, open licensing, transparent training data. I have a lot of things involved and they don't necessarily mean lower costs or commercial license or whatever.

So depending on what you're doing, you need massive data or you want to get trace out of big models to train smaller models. Thing is, I think it's still more of a craft than, an art thing than a process. So people are discovering this. And although you have the process for training models and for training things, applying that to your real world problems is still a process of discovery. So they end up spending a lot of money. I think that comes naturally. It's R&D basically.

Model Distillation [17:09]

Srini Penchikala: Yes. Hopefully some of these learnings from these companies will be shared with the community next year, the next couple years as Arthur you mentioned. Yes, I want to maybe talk a little bit about the model distillation topic. Chip, I know you talk about this in your book titled “AI Engineering”. I highly recommend everybody to check out the book by Chip, one of the very valuable books in the AI space. So you talk about model distillation. Can you discuss how it works and how it can help the overall model usage?

Chip Huyen: Yes. So I think model distillation is extremely important. It's very exciting. And I think a lot of us today benefit from model distillations either done by some providers or some application developers. So the idea is that you have a very big model that performs really, really well. But of course these big models are very expensive to run and of course a lot of them are very slow. So can we just get another smaller model to imitate a load from these big models so that you can achieve comparable or most comparable performance, but at a much cheaper price.

So a lot of time you can get, so we care about something called compute efficiency. So we usually think about, "Okay, for this much drop in the compute efficiency, how much is the performance we have to sacrifice?" And this metric has gone really, really, really well in recent years. I think that people are aggressively developing a lot of new techniques and it's working things that I didn't think would be possible even just a few years ago.

Srini Penchikala: Also in the models we have local versus on the cloud models, right? We can run some of these models locally using Ollama or the other LLM engines. And also these are multimodal models for the text and images. So anybody have any comments on those topics running these models on-prem versus cloud or the multimodal models?

Arthur Casals: I think regardless of the objective of defining what you're using, you need to separate a few questions about what we're doing because have you seen people defining on-prem versus cloud as a full thing or really separate, really binary thing. I mean, it depends on where the client runs, where the model runs, where the prompts to outputs, logs go, who keeps them. Everything's involved.

So in the end, both setups tend towards a hybrid approach. They're neither fully on-prem or in the cloud. And thing is, why is it important to define that for the company? What are they trying to solve? Is this a budget problem? Is this an architecture problem? So I mean, okay, you can categorize them, but what for, what are we doing with it? So which questions are you asking about this? It's not as simple as choosing a category and that's it.

Srini Penchikala: Thanks, Arthur. Yes, definitely a lot of other stuff happening. One thing I just want to mention briefly about the Jev model side, these are what they call System One models. I just started learning about these. I have no in-depth knowledge on this, but yes, I think we will definitely share more about this in the future. But has anybody else done any reading on this, like this Jev model from TypeSafe AI that they talk about very fast inference and very low cost compared to the LLMs?

Arthur Casals: Yes, it's supposed to be my weekend experiment for tomorrow.

Srini Penchikala: Cool.

Hien Luu: I've been watching a lot of videos on this and recently I watched a podcast from Latent Space where they interviewed the founder of TypeSafe. Very, very fascinating piece of technology. One of the key things I took away from that is a different type model, but it's also extremely fast. I think that's going to help unlock an interesting new sets of use cases.

There are a bunch of interesting demos about using that kind of decision to build UI and other use cases that you might have not considered like, "Hey, is that a relevant use case?" But it's a lot for us to learn and figure out how to incorporate this. But I think the key idea is, at least for the founder, is what he wanted to do is to build a model that is for builders and the output is for software, not for human. That's one of the key things he pointed out.

Srini Penchikala: It basically evaluates the state and returns the answers, and is mainly for the software. So we can maybe... Hien, you mentioned about the inference. I heard the same thing from my own experience. 2026 is being dubbed as the year of inference, right? So could you talk about how we are shifting from training models to running AI inference and what does all this mean in the real world usage? What are you seeing in terms of inference frameworks?

Hien Luu: Totally. The inference topics, I mean, it's exploded since beginning 2026. Obviously from one end, you have all these inference stack from vLLM, SGLang, and so on that are helping the rest of us to spin up our own inference service in our own environment. And at the same time, these open-weight models are becoming more and more capable. And that space is initially not a whole lot of people how it works and how to operate it, but now there's a lot more information and resources out there about how to actually use these software, how to optimize them. And at the same time, some of the use cases we talk about the financial companies where you have PIIs.

So the ability to host these open-weight models internally for those kinds of specific use cases are very, very relevant. And I believe that that's going to continue to grow, continue to be the case where a company will do more of this moving forward now that it's a lot more approachable, easier to do. There are some companies that because they want to save cost, they actually want to host internal open-weights models for coding, for example. So for many reasons that inference is going to continue to be a very, very useful, very powerful topic and more and more companies will start doing this moving forward in my mind.

Chip Huyen: Hien, it's very exciting for the work on inference. Do you have a focus on specific chips or hardware architecture to inference on?

Hien Luu: Not so much at this point because AMD is just coming online, but more and more inference providers, at least the neocloud, they want to be able to do inference across chips, Nvidia and AMDs and potentially in the future, Intels and so on. But at the moment, still predominantly Nvidia from what I gather.

Chip Huyen: I'm curious because I think this is a trend of as you get newer and newer chips, more powerful chips, there's many, many, many older generation of chips. And if somebody say, they almost come for free because they are so slow to run and so energy inefficient. So what do we do with them? So I think getting those done on older generation of chips, making things faster could be very interesting.

Having smaller, I think it tied more installations. You got to have smaller, cheaper models that require less complete footprint. You can fit them onto an older generation of chips. And also a lot of upcomers for chip because it's very hard to compute Nvidia on the flagship architecture, but you can definitely compete at a lower tier architecture.

Srini Penchikala: That probably the next area of the competition. I heard companies like Nvidia and Apple are definitely dominating the hardware space in terms of demand.

Hien Luu: Cerebras is an interesting chip player, and I think we'll see more of that maybe later on this year.

Context Engineering [24:57]

Srini Penchikala: Hien and Chip, you mentioned in a previous conversation about agentic loops and harness engineering and context engineering. Can you share, maybe starting with Chip you, can you share what you see happening in the context engineering space?

Chip Huyen: I do think definitely in the last couple of years, agentic coding use cases have been dominating everything. But I think with the TypeSafe launch, it shows that actually people have been so focused on coding. That's a huge tap area for non-coding use cases. For me, coding is definitely very important, but I definitely realize it's not the only thing.

Srini Penchikala: Yes. Arthur, what are your thoughts?

Arthur Casals: Context pollution is actually the biggest problem, the problem worth emphasizing now, because we've seen the past year or so movements toward bigger context windows in general, but they don't really solve the issue if the system cannot distinguish what's useful, what's current, what's alternative information from irrelevant, stale, adversarial material. So I'm bringing something from my own research here, but in general, more context can make an agent slower, more expensive, less reliable.

So the practical question would be, if you have your context window, regardless of the size of it, what enters the context? From which source, with which permission, for what step of the workflow so you don't have this huge pollution. That talks to retrieval quality, source distribution, professions rules, context model in general, context compression. So I mean, there's a huge, huge heap of problems underneath the word context. That's how I see it.

AI Agents [26:36]

Srini Penchikala: Thanks for saying that, Arthur. So yes, in the interest of time, I do want to move to other topics. I want to focus on the agents and the evals a little bit more in this discussion. So we can jump into the AI agents topic. Daniel, I know you've been looking into this space for a while now, so this continues to be one of the major trends in the AI space. Agents, they have gone, like you mentioned earlier, from just coding assistants and now they can act on several different aspects.

Daniel Dominguez: AI agents are probably one of the biggest trends of 2026. What I find interesting is that agents are moving through several levels very quickly. So we started with personal agents helping one person, then we start seeing agents working with teams, and now companies are thinking about agents operating across entire organizations. So I think the important change is that we're moving from beyond just a chatbot model. Instead, we are simply generating an answer. An agent can have goals, can use tools, can interact with software, can make decisions, can keep working until the task is complete.

So I think that changes AI from interface into something closer to an execution layer. We can see this mainly in software development. Software development is probably where this transition is more visible. So we move from autocomplete to copilots and now we have coding agents. We have tools like Claude, Codex, Cursor, Replit, and others that can navigate repositories, can modify multiple files, can run comments, can execute tasks, can inspect failures, and can iterate on their own. So the interesting question is no longer, can AI write code? We already know that AI can write code.

So there's AI governance platforms that are coming up and then there's AI security and regulations is an important topic. AI observability is an evolving topic as well. And definitely the AI SRE and AI ops are also getting a lot of attention. So do you see anything else happening at very high level before we wrap up? Arthur, do you have any comments?

Arthur Casals: Yes, I think we could relating multi-agent systems and AI engineering because not as hopeless that might have seen when it's reship, but there's a lot of things that we could bind together and bring together to correlate to how we solve problems that we have using work that has already been developed. So that would be a great topic.

Wrap Up and Predictions for Next Year

Srini Penchikala: We can start wrapping up. So this is my favorite part of the podcast to request each panelist to make a prediction for next year and we'll take a checkpoint next year and see how these predictions have been realized. So yes, we can start off with Chip, what do you see? What's your prediction? If there is one thing you'd like to see happen or you think is going to happen in the AI space, what would it be?

Chip Huyen: I really want to see US robot companies that have robots ready to be bought. I know it's just very painful. I feel like in China you can just buy a robot, in the US you just cannot get from an American company yet. So I really want to see that shipping. I feel like we've been waiting for OpenAI and Anthropic IPOs for a while. I think they delay. Very curious to see how that's going to impact the market because if the IPOs go well, is the market going to go well, but if IPOs don't go well, what implication would it have for the funding and the AI market? I would expect to see a lot of cheaper and faster models, the TypeSafe style of model would be very interesting.

Srini Penchikala: Thank you. How about you, Daniel? What's your prediction?

Daniel Dominguez: I think we're going to start seeing limitations on AI. So for example, the phrase is going to be the energy. So all the AI infrastructure is becoming extremely power hungry. So I think the access for electricity, the capacity, cooling data center locations, that is going to become a biggest constraint for the growth of AI. So we may start seeing energy crisis for AI. The second prediction that I would like to share is like a futuristic prediction, but I think it's going to happen that all this AI infrastructure is going to start moving beyond the traditional data center and it's going to move into space. So I think putting AI into space is going to be more efficient, probably it's going to take a little longer, but it's going to be more efficient than keeping the AI here on earth.

And finally, I think the AI competition between the United States and China is going to increasingly look like a technological Cold War. So it's not about who has the best model anymore or who has the best chips. So it has to be with who has the manufacturer, who has the energy, who has the data center, who has the open models, the supply chains, and the access to compute. So we are already seeing that semiconductor access and domestic chip productions are becoming strategic issues in that relationship. So I think that for 2027, some of the biggest AI stories may actually happen outside the models themselves. And it's going to be more about the energy, the chips, the infrastructure, and on the geopolitics.

Srini Penchikala: And Hien?

Hien Luu: Just two things. Every AI agent will incorporate some form of the Jev model into the AI agents. And more and more of the communications are going to be between agent and agents moving forward as we figure out how to build, operate and bring all these agents to production.

Srini Penchikala: And Arthur?

Arthur Casals: I'll circle back to what I said at the beginning. I think and I expect that the most successful AI deployments that we will see will be much narrower than what we see right now in terms that rather than one agent with access to everything, we'll see a lot of things using smaller specialized agents for mixed models, for well-defined tasks. And the big difference will be in the surrounding system.

So you have trusted data, leave the permissions tests, and does it not back your visibility, but a way to see what the agent did and whether it's actually helped. Teams can not only do that, but can actually measure the cost and quality of a completed task. You can have ROI for tasks, not just the number of tokens of agents that use it. I think that this will be a great leap.

It aligns well with what Hien said on Jev and what Daniel said on the shifting away from big models, but I think that's where I put my chips in.

Srini Penchikala: Thanks, Arthur. Yes, I think I'll take a quick one minute to wrap up my comments. AI is a significant technology shift. And as we all know by now, after almost four years, it is not a fad or some temporary blip on the technology radar. It is here to stay. It is one of the major technology waves in the last, I don't know, 20-plus years. So my advice and request to our audience is we should take advantage of this technology transformation, not be afraid of it. Find ways to use AI tools to automate any workflows in your day-to-day life, whether it is in the office or in your personal life.

I mean, this is a tool that we can use to find more time to do the important things in our lives, let the agents and the tools do the routine tasks. So my prediction for next year is definitely, I agree with all of you, AI will be even a bigger part of our daily lives. And I always say this as a prediction, and I would like to see whenever we don't talk about AI anymore, it has become part of the fabric of our lives. I think then we can say we have really arrived. And so I think maybe more evolution, more development, but I think the niche areas will be settled where AI will be really valuable and where human intelligence is still required.

So thank you all for your time. We took a little bit longer, but there are so many topics and we can go on forever, but I think we need to wrap this up and we will follow up with any other topics later. So thank you for joining today. Have a great one. Until next time, thank you.

entries.title: Microsoft Retires Azure Deployment Environments with No Replacement Product
entries.summary: Azure Deployment Environments retires on February 22, 2027 and Microsoft names no successor, telling teams to use Bicep or ARM templates directly. Microsoft Dev Box follows on September 18, 2028, pointed at Windows 365, which Microsoft says is not a one-to-one replacement. Remaining Dev Box workloads should expect deletion. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
entries.content:
Microsoft is retiring both halves of its Azure developer-environment offering. Azure Deployment Environments goes on February 22, 2027, with no successor product. Microsoft Dev Box follows on September 18, 2028, pointed at Windows 365, which Microsoft states plainly is not an equivalent.

The Deployment Environments retirement guide lists alternatives, and none of them is a product. Microsoft suggests "direct infrastructure-as-code deployment with Azure Resource Manager templates or Bicep," reusable Azure verified modules "when teams need standardized, governed building blocks," and CI/CD workflows "when environment provisioning can be integrated into repositories and pipelines." On the partner ecosystem it is blunter: "None of the third-party solutions we identified directly support a Bicep or ARM lifecycle. Use Bicep or ARM directly in Azure for deployment."

That is a hyperscaler leaving the environment-as-a-service category and telling customers to hand-roll what the product did. Microsoft says nothing about why it is withdrawing.

InfoQ covered the general availability in May 2023, when Microsoft launched the service at Build as the answer to exactly that problem. Senior program manager Sagar Chandra Reddy Lankala wrote then that "by enabling self-service deployment for developers, Azure Deployment Environments also benefits platform engineers," who could publish a catalog of standardized, pre-approved templates instead of provisioning environments one by one.

The service itself was free, with customers paying only for the Azure resources their environments created.

Self-service from a governed catalog is the capability going away, and it is the one the retirement guide does not replace. Bicep, verified modules, and pipelines rebuild the provisioning. They do not rebuild the catalog, the role rules, or the developer-facing portal. That territory belongs to Backstage, Port and Humanitec now.

Engineer Ikiru Yoshizaki, posting in Japanese as guitarrapc_tech, made the same objection from the user side when the retirement guide appeared. The advantage, he wrote, lay in the areas that could not be done easily with Bicep, Terraform or Pulumi. He did not spare the product either, adding that right to the end the API was unstable and the documentation sparse, and calling it sad that the value was never recognized.

Teams have sixteen months. Microsoft’s instruction is to inventory "ADE environments, definitions, catalogs, environment types, projects, dev centers, deployment subscriptions, identities, and role assignments," using the Azure Advisor Service Retirement workbook to find them, then validate a replacement for each scenario and move users and automation across. What happens on the date is only partly specified: "ADE create, deploy, redeploy, and other write operations are expected to be blocked. Inventory, read, log, and delete operations are planned to remain available for a time-bound cleanup period." How long that period runs is not stated.

Dev Box has a longer runway, though its clock started earlier than the headline date suggests. The service "starts its closing-down period at 16:00 UTC on 14 September 2026," more than a month ago, before full retirement at 17:00 UTC on 18 September 2028.

Microsoft’s own FAQ is unusually direct about what the move involves. Asked whether Windows 365 is a one-to-one replacement, the guide answers: "No. Windows 365 is the recommended path forward, but architecture, licensing, management, networking, image delivery, and developer self-service can differ. Validate each workload and don’t assume complete feature parity." Developer self-service is on that list, and it is the capability that made Dev Box a developer-platform product rather than managed desktops.

InfoQ covered the Dev Box general availability in July 2023, when that model ran on three roles: infrastructure admins handled security and networking, dev team leads built pools per project, and developers took boxes from enabled pools themselves. Amanda Silver, then corporate vice president in the Developer Division, said more than 10,000 Microsoft developers were using it internally.

There is no migration tool either. Teams should "provision the target Cloud PCs, recreate required policies and configurations, deploy applications, and transfer user data through approved processes." And the consequence of missing the date is stated without hedging: "Microsoft Dev Box won’t be available after retirement. Expect deletion of remaining customer workloads."

Windows 365 is a Microsoft 365 product rather than an Azure service, managed through Intune and licensed separately. Teams that adopted Dev Box as Azure infrastructure, billed and governed alongside the rest of their estate, are being moved to a different commercial surface. Azure Virtual Desktop, Microsoft’s Azure-native virtual desktop service, is not named anywhere in the retirement guide, though it remains under active development and reached a general availability milestone as recently as September.

The retirements are also entangled, since both products share dev center and project resources. The Deployment Environments guide warns against deleting shared dev centers "until you confirm that they have no remaining Microsoft Dev Box dependency."

Neither guide explains the withdrawal. The Dev Box notice says investment is going to Windows 365. For Deployment Environments there is no equivalent statement, only a list of things to build yourself.

entries.title: Google Adopts DPoP to Strengthen OAuth 2.0 against Token Theft and Replay Attacks
entries.summary: Google's OAuth Platform has recently introduces support for Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession (DPoP), an OAuth 2.0 security mechanism designed to mitigate token theft and replay attacks. By Sergio De Simone
entries.content:
Google's OAuth Platform has recently introduces support for Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession (DPoP), an OAuth 2.0 security mechanism designed to mitigate token theft and replay attacks.

Traditional OAuth bearer tokens operate on a "finders-keepers" model, making them vulnerable to Infostealer malware (e.g. RedLine, NodeStealer) and Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) attacks.

To prevent this types of attacks, DPoP uses cryptography to bind tokens to an asymmetric key pair generated by the client. Consequently, a stolen token cannot be replayed without the corresponding private key, which remains under the client’s control.

Google OAuth platform supports DPoP only for refresh tokens, while access tokens, which are shorter-lived, remain standard Bearer tokens. This decision is motivated by the fact that long-lived refresh tokens are "the primary vector for persistent online impersonation", whereas applying DPoP to access tokens would introduce "asymmetric cryptographic verification overhead" for each request.

It is worth noting that adopting DPoP adds several client-side requirements, including generating cryptographic keys, handling timestamps and nonces correctly, generating the appropriate HTTP headers and the required DPoP proof JWTs.

While DPoP provides protection for API tokens, it does not protect standard web application session cookies, which remain vulnerable to Infostealer malware. To address the threat of cookie theft, Google and the Web Incubator Community Group (WICG) are developing Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC).

DBSC operates at the browser and network layer to cryptographically bind browser session cookies to the device's hardware (such as TPM). Together, DPoP and DBSC form a comprehensive defense-in-depth strategy against credential theft across both API and web-based user sessions.

Google also notes that DPoP is not appropriate for multi-agent workflows, as one agent cannot easily delegate a task to another agent. This would in fact require the second agent to sign requests on behalf of the first. However, this in not possible without accessing the private key generated by the first agent, which would violate DPoP. As an alternative, Google recommends developers to consider Google Cloud Secure Token Service (STS).

By routing delegation through STS, the intermediate agent can exchange the upstream token for a new, short-lived federated token cryptographically bound to its own local key pair, preserving the sender-constrained security model across the entire agent chain without key exposure.

Since the DPoP private key is stored client-side, its security ultimately depends on the security of the client itself. However, as Dhruv Agnihotri argues, single-page-apps (SPAs) running inside a browser are not entirely protected against misuse of the key. The IETF's guidance for browser-based applications therefore recommends adopting the Backend-for-Frontend pattern to keep tokens and cryptographic keys out of the browser. Agnihotri also proposes a zero-persistence approach, which may be useful when server-side infrastructure is unavailable.

entries.title: Bug0 Releases QA Agent to Automate Regression Testing With Cached Playwright Replays
entries.summary: QA Agent is a new source-available Playwright library for agentic browser regression testing. The agent associates test instructions expressed in natural language to actions on the user interface, caches those when appropriate for faster CI replays, remapping them to test specifications when the user interface changes. Verification is based on multi-model consensus and vision model evaluations. By
entries.content:
Linearbytes released Bug0 QA Agent, a source-available Playwright library for agentic browser regression testing. The AI agent associates the test instructions expressed in natural language to actions on the user interface, caches those when appropriate for faster CI replays, remapping them to test specifications when the user interface changes. Verification is based on consensus from up to three LLMs and evaluations from vision models.

At one end of the spectrum, legacy approaches to web application testing, while largely automated, do not incorporate AI as a key productivity factor. At the other extremity, innovative teams follow a fully agent-based automated approach to testing where the agent is front and center, handling every browser interaction dynamically.

The legacy approaches often falls prey to known pain points. Test suites commonly depend on implementation details (CSS classes, attributes, data-testid) that may change even when the specifications remain constant, causing unnecessary test rewriting and refactoring. Flaky tests result from the inherently inpredictible nature of the complex, asynchronous and distributed systems underlying web applications (race conditions, latency, dropped calls).

AI-first testing approaches on the other hand suffer from high latency that makes them impractical for large regression suites. LLMs can routinely add several seconds of latency per step, escalate API token costs, and introduce their own brand of flakyness due to the non-determinism of the actions performed. On the bright side, test generation resists well to changes in the implementation; image and video models may provide visual verification with some success.

Bug0 proposes an hybrid approach in which its autonomous agent decouples the initial visual exploration from routine regression execution. Developers write declarative test steps in plain English inside standard Playwright specs.

test("Shopping cart tests", async ({ page }) => {
  await runSteps({
    page,
    test,
    expect,
    userFlow: "Add product to cart",
    steps: [
      { description: "Navigate to https://demo.vercel.store" },
      { description: "Click Acme Circles T-Shirt" },
      { description: "Select color", data: { value: "White" } },
      { description: "Select size", data: { value: "M" } },
      { description: "Add to cart", waitUntil: "My Cart is visible" },
    ],
    assertions: [{ assertion: "Cart shows the Acme Circles T-Shirt" }],
  });
});

During an initial execution, the agent inspects the accessibility tree and screenshots to understand the user interface and perform the requested actions. Once a single-action step executes successfully, the framework compiles the interaction into concrete browser operations and caches them into an in-memory Redis store. On following runs, the suite replays the cached action directly through Playwright, eschewing the latency cost of a new LLM inference.

When implementation details of the user interface change (e.g., button coordinates updated, form hierarchies modified), the replayed Playwright action may as a result throw an execution failure. Rather than failing the entire test run, Bug0 QA Agent detects the break, invalidates the action cache, and re-invokes the multimodal agent loop. Important caveat: caching applies only to single-action steps; complex, multi-action directives re-execute through the agent on every run.

Unlike action steps, assertion verification is not cached. Assertions execute through vision models on every pass. Claude and Gemini independently evaluate every assertion, with a third model breaking ties. Video models allow catching transient UI defects (e.g., auto-dismissing toast alerts, flashing banner errors).

The framework embeds disposable email testing via mailsink and community-built adapters like Mailinator, allowing tests to extract one-time passwords (OTPs) and magic links via natural language prompts like 

{{email.otp:Extract the 6-digit code}}
.

Chevrot et al. (Are Autonomous Web Agents Good Testers?) reports that their best-performing autonomous testing architecture (ATA) agreed with human professional testers for only about 60% of test runs, identifying assertion verifiability and grounding (identification of the relevant elements of the target application for the test action) as primary drivers of improvement to scale usage of autonomous testing agents. The paper was published in April 2025 and used GPT-4o, Sonnet, and Gemini. As language models and harnesses regularly improve, so do the efforts to use AI to improve the productivy of testing in all its aspects (generation, self-healing, execution, triage, analytics).

Bug0 QA Agent is released under the Functional Source License, Version 1.1, ALv2 Future License. The Functional Source License is a source-available license (i.e., not open-source), that imposes non-compete restrictions during the first two years of usage. The license came of existence to, in the words of Sentry, its first proponent, “grant freedom without harmful free-riding.”

entries.title: How to Make Artificial Intelligence More Environmentally Sustainable
entries.summary: IT is responsible for about 2 - 4% of all global emissions, and electricity use at Microsoft and Google has climbed because of AI, according to their own reports. Sustainability ought to be a top-level architectural concern. Some recommendations are: use pre-built and smaller models, run compute where low-carbon electricity is abundant, and train on renewable energy. By Ben Linders
entries.content:
IT is responsible for about 2 - 4% of all global emissions, and electricity use at Microsoft and Google has climbed because of AI, according to their own reports. Charles Humble spoke about Green AI at GOTO Copenhagen, where he argued sustainability ought to be a top-level architectural concern. Amongst his recommendations: use pre-built and smaller models, run compute where low-carbon electricity is abundant, and train on renewable energy.

Humble quoted the International Energy Agency (IEA), which has stated that the combined electricity use from Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta has more than doubled between 2017 and 2021, rising to around 72 terawatt-hours in 2021. Microsoft’s 2024 environmental report mentioned that its total carbon emissions have risen 30% since 2020, primarily due to the construction of data centers to meet demand for AI. Google’s emissions had surged about 50% since 2019 and 13% year on year in 2023 alone, according to their own reporting, largely driven by artificial intelligence.

The emission that these reports talk about is mainly carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. Since the Industrial Revolution we’ve been increasing the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, trapping more heat, Humble said. We want to keep our warming to 1.5 degrees by 2100, but projections suggest that it will be between about 2.5 and 3 degrees.

The IT industry contributes a lot to this problem, partly through electricity use as Humble explained:

The IEA estimated that global data centre electricity consumption in 2022 is about 240 to 340 terawatt hours, 1 to 1.3% of global electricity demand. Networks add another 260 to 360 terawatt hours. That’s 700 terawatt hours, about the same as Brazil’s 726 terawatt hours in the same time period.

IT is responsible for about 2 - 4% of all global emissions, where aviation is 3%, Humble said. But while the aviation industry is working quite hard to try and cut its emissions, we as an industry are doing the opposite.

There are several questions Humble suggested asking for putting AI into a business context:

  • Do you really need it?
  • Do you need to train a new model from scratch, or can you use a pre-built one?
  • If you can relax part of your SLA, does that allow you to run your workloads in a greener location?
  • Can you use demand shaping?

If we need to train a custom model, Humble suggested thinking about how much data we actually need to collect. Sometimes, smaller models work better, he argued. He also suggested using open-source data sets and, if possible, demand shifting to collect data when and where there is green energy available.

In theory, training can be on 100% renewable energy all the time, which can reduce carbon emissions somewhere between 45% and 99%, Humble mentioned.

He argued that most of the energy may actually be spent when we deploy a model into production and maintain it, and mentioned four steps to make all computing greener:

  • Use the smallest hardware configuration that can safely execute the job.
  • Run compute in areas where low-carbon electricity is abundant and where there are credible plans to make the grid even cleaner.
  • Use cloud services from cloud providers that have data centers in green locations and provide good tooling to help reduce your footprint.
  • Optimize the execution time of jobs to further reduce the carbon footprint.

Sustainability ought to join cost, performance, security, regulatory concerns, and reliability as one of the top-level considerations for your computing workloads, Humble concluded. We should think about how to build systems in a more environmentally sound way.

InfoQ interviewed Charles Humble after his talk.

InfoQ: How does location matter when it comes to reducing carbon emissions?

Charles Humble: A compute workload uses a fixed amount of energy, but the carbon cost of that energy varies enormously by place and time depending on the sources of electricity that is powering the data centre. Assuming the data centre is using grid power in a region running mostly on hydro, solar, nuclear and wind (for example Norway, Sweden and France), running a workload here can be many times cleaner than one dependent on coal or gas. Carbon intensity also changes during the day and over the course of the year as wind, solar and demand vary.

In carbon aware computing we can apply a technique called demand shifting based on this. Demand shifting can be done in one of two ways, either time or location based. Time-based is particularly applicable when a use case isn’t latency sensitive, such as AI training.

For location the most simple variation of the technique is to just pick lower-carbon regions by default for new, latency-tolerant workloads. More advanced variations might involve moving to different hemispheres seasonally to maximize exposure to sunlight and solar power.

InfoQ: How does demand shaping work?

Humble: Demand shaping means changing how much work your software does, or what kind of work, in response to how clean or constrained the electricity supply is at that moment. One version of this is to give users a choice. For an AI-powered service, you could let users choose to talk to a person instead of the AI up front, or at any point during the process.

You can also apply techniques such as graceful degradation based on higher carbon intensity, for example by serving lower-quality video or images, turning off autoplay, skipping non-essential animations, or reducing refresh rates. You might also use a smaller model.

Tradeoffs include increased complexity, and of course you have to determine if the reduced service is still acceptable.

InfoQ: What can we do to make model training greener?

Humble: Alongside demand shifting for both training and data collection, avoid training from scratch if at all possible. Use a pre-trained model and fine-tune it, or just prompt it and/or use Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) if that meets the need.

Shrinking the model size can speed up training and improve efficiency. Distillation, quantization and pruning can all be used for compression. On-device training via Federated learning can be greener in some cases. Keep in mind that for widely used models, inference over the model’s lifetime may cause greater total emissions, so efficiency in serving matters too.

Raghavendra Selvan’s book "Sustainable AI" explores a number of these approaches in considerably greater depth, so if readers want to learn more, this is a great resource.
